**Plumbing re-cut with no checkout (`e10.sh`).** `T=$(git merge-tree --write-tree --merge-base=C^ O C)`, then `git commit-tree $T -p O` with the original message gives a one-commit suggestion whose parent is the owner's tip. `git update-ref refs/ddflow/suggest/O/S1 $N` stores it. `git diff --stat O S1` showed 1 line changed, the contributor's author kept. This costs a few ms and needs no worktree.

**Dirty owner tree.** Cherry-pick worked with an unrelated dirty file and refused on a dirty same file. Plain `git diff O S1 | git apply` applied disjoint hunks onto the dirty file as uncommitted changes. `git apply --3way` failed with "does not match index" on a dirty file. So the owner-side apply needs a fallback ladder: cherry-pick, else `git apply`, else send back.

**Idempotence by accident.** Cherry-picking onto the same parent in the same second reproduced the identical sha (same author, committer, date, tree). Do not rely on that.

**Semantic conflict that applies cleanly (`e9.sh`).** The contributor added `helper(1)`. The owner renamed `helper` to `helper2` elsewhere. `merge-tree` said CLEAN and the merge ran with no markers. Running the result then gave `NameError: name 'helper' is not defined`. A clean probe proves textual applicability only. The owner's gates and ci on the result are mandatory.

### Syncing the contributor with the owner's progress (`e7.sh`)

C was reviewed at `53239de`, tree `f698a0a`, patch-id `ad7d72e078`. O then got two commits.

| Strategy | What changed | Effect on a review of C |
|---|---|---|
| A. Merge O into C | New merge commit `ccfc838`, tree `09602a2`. The reviewed sha is still an ancestor. | The tree changed, so tree-keyed gate outcomes are stale. This is what `ddflow sync` does today. |
| B. Rebase C onto O | Sha `e7ebb6c`. Patch-id still `ad7d72e078`. The reviewed sha is no longer an ancestor. | The tree changed and the sha is lost. This needs the DX-sync-rebase alias map and the unpublished-branch restriction. |
| C. C stays; the suggestion is re-cut on O's tip | C untouched (still `53239de`). Probe printed `clean`. | An in-flight review of C is not disturbed. |

**Least risky:** C. C stays based on main, and only the suggestion is re-cut against O's tip, via the `commit-tree` recipe above. Fall back to A if the contributor itself must continue working on top of O's changes. B is the riskiest.

### After the owner merges to main (`e7.sh`)

| Owner landing | `git cherry main S` | `git rebase main` in the contributor |
|---|---|---|
| Cherry-picked unchanged, ff-merged | `-` (applied) | "skipped previously applied commit". Succeeds with nothing left. |
| Cherry-picked unchanged, squashed into one commit | `+` (patch-id differs) | "dropping … patch contents already upstream". Also succeeds with nothing left. |
| Owner tweaked the suggestion | `+` | `Could not apply bfd0a88… suggest line20`. Conflict. The contributor must drop it or re-send. |

So the contributor's rule is: `git rebase main`. If it ends empty, close the suggestion as applied. If it conflicts, show the diff against main and let the contributor drop or re-send. `git cherry` alone is not enough (it misses squashes). Combine it with a check that `merge-tree` of main and the suggestion equals main's tree.

### Per-method summary

| Method | One machine | Remote or container | Authorship and provenance | Idempotent | Detects "already applied" | Owner changed the lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| cherry-pick -x | yes | no | author kept, `-x` line | stops with "empty" | by patch-id | conflict, rerere helps repeats |
| merge | yes | no | full history | yes | yes | conflict |
| format-patch + am -3 | yes | yes | author kept | "already applied" | yes | conflict, `--abort` |
| hidden ref | yes | with refspec | commit is the proof | yes | patch-id | n/a |
| bundle | yes | yes | commit is the proof | yes | patch-id | n/a |
| trailers | yes | yes | yes | n/a | n/a | n/a |
| notes | yes | refspec | lost on cherry-pick | n/a | n/a | n/a |

If the owner rebases or squashes, a `refs/ddflow/suggest/...` ref stays valid (the suggestion commit is not on the owner's branch). A merge of C would be rewritten by a rebase, and `git cherry` can no longer match after a squash.

## PART 3. Protocol design

### Design principle

A suggestion is a RECORD (event log is the blackboard) that points at a git ref. The inbox carries only a fenced pointer message, and git carries the patch. This keeps "workers do not message each other" true in the sense that matters. The patch is data, never an instruction.

### Recommended protocol spec

```
# --- records (templates/events/handoff.toml; folded into State.suggestions) ---
suggestion.proposed  id from_item from_agent to_item to_agent(lease holder now) base(sha cut on)
                     ref patch_id files[] +lines -lines kind(fix|gate_fix|refactor|doc) reason
                     probe{clean,tip,ms} blob? (format-patch in .ddflow/blobs) evidence?(cmd,exit)
suggestion.seen      id            (written by ddflow when delivered at any door)
suggestion.accepted  id            (owner will apply; optional)
suggestion.applied   id commit patch_id tip          (owner, or ddflow when patch-id lands in the branch/main)
suggestion.rejected  id reason     (owner; reason required, <=500 chars)
suggestion.countered id new_id reason (owner edited it; old closed, new proposed back to the sender)
suggestion.withdrawn id            (sender)
suggestion.superseded id by        (sender re-cut; or ddflow when the same sender re-sends)
suggestion.expired   id action(task|none) task?   (ddflow, from ttl or owner merge-ready/gone)

# --- state machine: who moves what ---
proposed -> seen            ddflow            seen -> accepted -> applied     owner
proposed|seen -> rejected|countered           owner (lease holder of to_item, or the next claimant)
proposed|seen -> withdrawn|superseded         sender          -> expired      ddflow only
any open -> any             operator (override)    sender cannot accept/apply; owner cannot expire.

# --- commands (CLI = MCP action; no shell needed) ---
ddflow suggest ITEM [--commit C | --diff | --blob F] --reason "..." [--kind gate_fix --evidence CMD,EXIT]
   -> re-cuts onto owner's tip with merge-tree/commit-tree, probes, writes ref, emits proposed
ddflow suggestion list|show S ; apply S ; reject S --reason ; counter S ; withdraw S
   apply = cherry-pick -x (fallback: git apply, then reject-with-reason); trailers added:
           Suggested-by: <sender> / ddflow-suggestion: S from=<item>@<agent> patch-id=<id>

# --- caps and limits ([handoff] knobs, r-everything-configurable) ---
enabled=false(until stage2) max_files=3 max_lines=60 max_bytes=65536 ttl_s=14400
max_open_per_sender=3 max_open_per_owner=10 min_interval_s=120 reject_breaker=3 (sender paused)
redact=true (staged-scan + secret redaction on diff before it is stored or shown)
auto_apply=off|tiny (stage 3) nudge_after_s=600 expire_action=task|none

# --- delivery (ddflow writes an inbox message reason="suggestion" pointing at the record) ---
doors in order: hook (PostToolUse / plugin tool.execute.after / UserPromptSubmit) reads ONLY the local inbox dir;
  heartbeat; wait/watch wake reason "suggestion"; brief/status line; coordinator relay (Lane.steer /
  SendMessage) when the owner is idle > nudge_after_s and kind=gate_fix; harnesses without hooks poll brief.

# --- gates and review ---
owner is author of record; contributor model joins the item's author families (reviewer must differ from all);
apply changes the tree: tree-keyed outcomes stale, rerun only gates whose paths overlap the applied files
(testselect on files from the suggestion); ci on the merge result mandatory (semantic conflicts are proven possible);
review sees the applied commit as a delta (range-diff vs the suggestion = "owner edited").
gate_fix open for a failed gate of to_item -> `merge`/`complete` refuse until accepted|rejected(+reason).
others unanswered at owner's queue-add or ttl -> expired(action=task: needs=[to_item], globs=files, body=patch ref).
```

### Exact next_actions text for the owner

The CLI is shown first, then the MCP form. This follows `r-tell-dont-discover` (a ready command, not a hint) and `r-no-shell` (works over MCP).

```
suggestion S1 from item PM-env@pm-env touches a.py:10-12 (+1 -1, kind fix), probe: clean on your tip ab12cd3 (8 ms)
  reason: <fenced text, untrusted data>
  apply  : ddflow suggestion apply S1        (MCP: ddflow_suggestion action=apply id=S1)
  reject : ddflow suggestion reject S1 --reason "..."   (MCP: action=reject id=S1 reason="...")
  look   : ddflow suggestion show S1                    (expires in 3h50m; unanswered becomes task sugg-S1)
```

For a `gate_fix` the first line adds `BLOCKS your merge: fixes failing gate ci (evidence: pytest tests/x -> exit 1)`. It is delivered as an inbox message with reason `suggestion` ordered after `yield`. The message text carries only the pointer and the one-line summary, never the patch.

### Sync and notify events

- **`drift.relevant`** is emitted by merge or the queue: item, paths, commit. It uses the DX-merge-fanout-notify design.
- **`peer.merge_ready`** is a new event, emitted at `queue add` or `pr`: item, paths. Receivers are live items whose changed, leased or reviewed paths intersect it. It is computed at emit time, with no subscription table.
- **`suggestion.*`** events reach the owner by the doors above.
- **Noise control:**
  - Silent for unrelated merges.
  - Coalesce per (receiver, source) within 60 s.
  - One line per receiver per door.
  - Cap at `[handoff].notice_max_per_hour`.
  - Severity: `info` (shown only in brief), `relevant`, `blocking` (gate_fix, or the receiver's lease is yield-requested).
- **What the receiver is told** (the next_actions line):
  - Unrelated drift: nothing.
  - Relevant drift before review starts: `ddflow sync`.
  - Relevant drift mid-review: continue; the sync point at pre_merge or the queue handles it.
  - `peer.merge_ready` touching your files: `ddflow sync --check`, then send your own change as a suggestion if the peer lands first.
  - Suggestion: apply or reject.

### Operational rules

- **Ownership:** owner = current lease holder of the item that declared or changed the file. First writer breaks ties. A directory owner is not used. If no lease is live, there is no owner and the contributor claims the file normally.
- **Threshold:** above `max_files` or `max_lines` it is an ordinary task (`task add`, patch attached), not a suggestion.
- **May ignore vs must not ignore.** The owner may reject any `fix`, `refactor` or `doc` with a one-line reason; silence just expires into a task. The owner must answer a `gate_fix` for its own failing gate; `merge` and `complete` refuse until it is accepted or rejected with a reason. A gate_fix needs recorded evidence (the failing command and exit code), as the evidence-required gates do.
- **Disputes:** operator override. A rejection that cites "the contributor was wrong" is just a reason; repeated rejections of the same sender trip the breaker.
- **Authority amendment:** record `D-handoff-peers`: an agent may send a suggestion to the lease holder of the file it needs. It is data, carries no authority, and is never an approval. This relaxes only the "agent may tell only its master" part of D-context-sync, and the operator should answer it.

### Failure modes and mitigations

- **Owner crashed or lease expired:** on a new claim of `to_item` by another holder, ddflow re-addresses open suggestions. If the item is abandoned or removed, `expired(action=task)` files `sugg-<id>`.
- **Owner merge-ready (queue add):** open non-gate_fix suggestions expire to tasks that need the owner item. The contributor can take the lock after the owner merges.
- **Loops (A suggests to B, who suggests back):** at most one open suggestion per (sender, owner) pair, and a suggestion cannot target an item that holds a suggestion to the sender on the same files. This is the same hop-limit idea as triggers.
- **Deadlock:** a pending suggestion creates no lock and no `needs` edge until it expires into a task. `r-lock-cycle-selfheal` is unaffected.
- **Semantic conflict:** the owner's gates and ci on the merge result are mandatory (shown above).
- **Flood and a weak model:** caps and the reject breaker above. Require the diff to apply to the tip (the probe), a reason, and for gate_fix an evidence command.
- **Secrets in patches:** run the staged-content scanner (GR-staged-scan, open) and the redactor on the diff before storing it in the log or blob. Refuse the suggestion if it matches a secret value.
- **Token cost:** the owner reads at most a bounded summary (files, hunks, `max_lines`) plus `suggestion show`. Reject cheaply with a reason. There is no LLM resolution step: a conflict is rejected or countered, never auto-resolved.
- **Stale ref:** if the owner tip moved, `merge-tree` is re-run on `apply`. If it now conflicts, ddflow says "stale: re-cut" and the sender is told to re-send (`superseded`).

### Interaction with the lock research

- **R-lock-landscape / R-lock-inventory ranked mechanisms** (lazy per-file lock, release at merge-ready/during gates, optimistic edits with merge-tree as arbiter) are enabled, not replaced. This protocol is the "someone else holds the file" outcome of lazy acquire: instead of waiting, send a suggestion. The `merge-tree` probe (8 ms) is the arbiter both designs already want.
- **DX-lease-hunk-optimistic** uses the same `merge-tree` check. Two disjoint-hunk edits can both proceed. Suggestions cover the overlapping case.
- **DAG optimizer:** an expired suggestion becomes a normal task with a `needs` edge on the owner item, so the optimizer schedules it (OPT-*). Suggestions do not enter the DAG while open.
- **Granular test runs:** the applied files feed `testselect`. **Merged/batched gates (BG-ci):** a batch gate runs on the combined tree anyway, so it already covers an applied suggestion.
- **Release during gate waits (LC-release):** the lane inbox keeps the offer for the lane's next wait, so a suggestion sent during a gate wait is not lost.

# 2. Local measurements

**Method.** I read the 762 JSONL files in `.ddflow/events` (51,416 non-heartbeat events). I looked at tasks with `item.completed` between 2026-10-19 07:42 UTC and 2026-11-02, which gave 490 completed tasks with a `lease.acquired`. Hold time runs from the first `lease.acquired` to the last `lease.released`, or to completion if there is no release. Merge facts come from `worktree.merged`: `landed_before` and `sha`, which is a true merge commit whose first parent is `landed_before`. Everything is read-only; scripts and pickles are in the scratchpad.

**(a) Lease hold time, n=490**
- Total hold: p50 2.3 h, p90 21.4 h, 3,825 lease-hours.
- Claim to merge (n=487): p50 106 min, p90 682 min.
- Claim to first gate start (n=408): p50 10.4 min, p90 57 min.
- Time inside non-review gates: p50 7.8 min, p90 79 min (6% of lease-hours).
- Time inside `rubber_duck` and `critic` reviews: p50 33 min, p90 117 min (11%).
- Last review end to release (n=403): p50 44 min, p90 14.9 h.
- 33.5% of lease-hours (1,282 h) fall after the merge. Median merge to release is 101 s, but p90 is 8 h, so a long tail of items stay leased after landing.
- The p90 values are inflated by idle or crashed holders. The brief lists 10 crashed worktrees and 29 leftovers, and those would not appear here because they never completed.
- First review start to merge: p50 104 min, 1,902 h summed. But **334 of 400 tasks (84%) commit again after their first review starts**, a median of 91 min after it. Releasing the lease at review start would therefore be wrong for most tasks.

**(b) Declared-glob precision, 100 random completed tasks.** I expanded the first claim's globs over the merge tree with my own regex and compared them to the merge's net diff.
- 50% of declared files (pooled) were never touched. Median expanded declared set is 2 files, but a few huge globs such as `docs/**` dominate the pooled share.
- 18% of globs matched no touched file.
- 45% of actually touched files were outside any declared glob, and 54 of 100 tasks wrote at least one undeclared file. The common undeclared paths are `tests/`, `tests/golden/__snapshots__/`, `README.md`, `ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/` and `ddflow/api/`.
- Caveats: I used the first claim's globs only, so later `task.updated` edits may have widened them. Glob regex semantics are approximate. The net diff includes conflict-resolution content.

**(c) Wait spans.** There are 427 `lease.waiting` events in total, 277 in the window. I merged consecutive events per item into spans: 144 spans in the window.
- 68 ended in `lease.acquired`, 58 in `lease.released`, 5 in `task.removed`, 2 in `item.abandoned`, and 11 are still open. The 58 releases probably mean the waiter gave up or was self-healed, so the end event is ambiguous.
- Total wait is 495 h (about 13% of the 3,825 lease-hours). For spans that ended, p50 is 5,443 s (91 min), p90 40,099 s (11.1 h), max 35 h.

**(d) False serialization.** 108 ended spans could be classified, because the waiter and all named blockers have merge diffs. These cover 456.6 wait-hours.
- 38 spans (145.4 h, 32% of classifiable hours) were between tasks whose **actual** changed file sets were disjoint. Median wait 55 min.
- The other 70 spans (311 h, median 2 h) had real file overlap in the net diffs.
- Blockers can be named only by `on[].item`, and the other 25 spans lacked a merge for one side.

**(e) Real conflicts**
- Pairs where A merged during B's life, using claim and merge times: 4,343. Of those, 538 had overlapping own-commit files.
- 212 of 487 tasks (44%) had main merged into their branch at some point, so their pairwise conflict can't be reconstructed. In 470 of the 538 pairs B had synced main.
- For the 68 evaluable pairs (B never synced), `git merge-tree --write-tree` of A's merge commit against B's tip gave **1 conflict and 67 clean (1.5%)**. The one conflict was DX-bug-repro-verify vs `fix-B66f6d0c93e` (`ddflow/api/review.py` among others). The 68 pairs cover only 36 distinct tasks, so this is a small sample.
- A separate sample of 60 in-branch main-merges: `git diff-tree --remerge-diff` was empty in all 60, so none needed manual resolution. The sample is capped at 3 merges per task, and a full run was too slow to finish.
- Hunk-level overlap was **not computed**. Two attempts were too slow or too contaminated by merged-in main content. I did not run a second hunk analysis.
- Higher-order proxy: 41 of 483 bugs filed in the window are "main red after merge" bugs (CI check failed or baseline-red). That is 8.4% of the 487 merges. Most examples are lint, gitleaks or ratchet failures. I did not split how many are true semantic collisions such as two tasks each adding a ratchet site.

**merge-tree cost (item 7)**
- Git 2.43.0. Repo has 23,476 commits, 4,225 files in the main tree, and a 114 MiB pack (162 MB `.git`).
- 27 `ddflow/*` branches vs main (best of 2 runs): median 16 ms, p90 1.29 s, max 2.6 s; 4 report conflicts. The slow ones are branches 11,644 to 18,394 commits behind (old, stale). Branches under 400 commits behind take 8–21 ms, with one 1.2 s outlier at 224 behind that looks like a cold cache.
- First, loaded-machine run, 20 branches: median 21 ms, p90 1.35 s, max 7.2 s.
- 10 random pairs of commits from the last 500: median 7 ms, 0 conflicts. 10 random pairs of branches: median 22 ms, 3 conflicts.
- 60 recent real merges, `sha^2` vs `sha^1`: median 13 ms, p90 15 ms.
- The largest branch available (ADP-census-v2, 25 commits ahead): 15 ms.
- Overall: the probe is cheap enough to run at every gate boundary.

# 3. What changes in the recommendations

**Reorder or drop**
1. **Drop "release at review start / merge-ready".** The 84% commit-after-review rate contradicts it. What is idle is the 33.5% of lease-hours after merge. Release the lease at merge, not at `complete`, as the first fix.
2. **Reduce false serialization before anything fancy.** 32% of classifiable wait-hours were between tasks whose real files were disjoint. Cheapest version: leases on declared-and-observed files, with undeclared writes detected at gate time against the lease. Falsifier: if red-main bugs or textual merge-tree conflicts rise above about 5% of merges, revert. The current baseline is 1.5% textual in the evaluable sample, 8.4% for red-main.
3. **Fix declared globs.** 45% of touched files are undeclared, which makes the lease an unreliable hint. Feed the observed file set back as the default declaration (`tests/`, golden snapshots and `README.md` are the usual misses). Falsifier: the share of undeclared files stays above 30% after one iteration.
4. **Keep leases, but demote them to scheduling hints.** Cursor measured locks as a throughput bottleneck and chose optimistic concurrency. Anthropic's compiler used task locks, and merge conflicts were "frequent". The external evidence supports hints plus an arbiter, not hard exclusion.
5. **Put a `git merge-tree --write-tree` probe at claim, at each gate start and at merge.** It is the arbiter. On 2.43.0 use `--name-only` and read the exit code; don't use `--quiet` (rc 129).
6. **Merge-queue style speculation** (Zuul or GitHub semantics) is lower priority: the log shows 1.5% pairwise textual conflict and 16 ms probes, so conflicts are not the bottleneck; waiting is.
7. **Mergiraf as an optional `*.py` merge driver.** Cheapest safe version: install it only in a scratch evaluation, and compare conflict counts on replayed merges. Falsifier: fewer than 10% of replayed textual conflicts solved, which is likely given the Linux kernel's 5.8%.
8. **Awareness (notify when an overlapping merge lands in your window).** Brun's data (20% of clean-merge risks turn into conflicts, persistence median 0.7 days) supports it. The cheapest version is a probe plus a notification at gate start. I found no field result showing it reduces conflicts.
9. **Dependency-aware scheduling** (writers of one module serialized, readers allowed). Cheapest version: drop read-only globs from leases. Falsifier: wait-hours unchanged after readers are exempted.
10. **Lock-free append-only logs with `merge=union`** is confirmed to work inside merge-tree. Fit: baselines, event shards and golden snapshot indexes, which are the frequent undeclared paths. Risk: union can silently keep both sides of a semantic collision.
11. **`git range-diff` after rebase** semantics are verified. Fit: skip re-review when the diff-of-diffs is empty. Cost: the creation-factor heuristic can misreport big edits as rewrites.
12. **`git rerere`** is verified but conflicts are rare here; low priority.
13. **Contract-first file splitting.** This repo's rule r-small-files already does it. Anthropic's compiler used a reference compiler (GCC) as an oracle to split work. Fit: high, already in place.
14. **CODEOWNERS plus bots** is verified as a review-routing tool only. It doesn't help lock hold time.
15. **Test-impact selection** is verified to exist with documented blind spots (data files, dependency changes). Meta reports over 99.9% of faulty changes caught at half the cost. Fit for Python is unproven: no miss rate is published for testmon or Datadog.
16. **"Pair-agent handoff" and "semantic locking via AST node ids"**: I found no evidence for either. Claim Plane is the nearest published idea and has only a six-pair feasibility check.

# 4. Hype list

- Any claim that worktrees prevent conflicts. They only defer them to merge time (secondary blog posts; the 41.7% cross-agent figure in arXiv 2607.04697 shows what that costs).
- Vendor percentages from Launchable ("up to 80% faster" and the demo workspace figures).
- "Mergiraf resolves conflicts": 5.8% fully on the Linux kernel, and correctness is unreported. Python has no figure.
- The 27.67% AgenticFlict rate treated as universal. It is textual-only, covers 75% of PRs, and has no human baseline.
- "LLMs resolve merge conflicts": under 60% correct on the best Merge-Bench models; ConGra's 80%-similarity bar overstates correctness.
- Agent-team size recommendations. Anthropic itself says 3–5 teammates; Cursor's "several hundred agents" ran with no integrator and accepted "turbulence".
- The 10–20% merge-conflict rate: Ghiotto cites it as a prior figure, so it is not an independent measurement.
- Uber's "40% problem chance" at 16 concurrent changes is from a secondary summary only.

# 5. Could not verify (carried into the note)

- Uber EuroSys 2019 PDF (ACM 403).
- Accioly 2018 per-merge conflict rate, and Ghiotto's own rate and chunk-count distribution.
- Any study linking conflict probability to branch lifetime or developer count.
- Perforce `+l` and `p4 opened -a` primary text.
- Crystal and Palantir effect sizes.
- Meta PTS full-paper test share.
- Google TAP skip fraction.
- Sapling auto-restack, Graphite, ghstack.
- GitHub suggested changes and Gerrit.
- Codex, Devin and OpenHands conflict handling.
- Cost per LLM conflict resolution.
- Hunk-level overlap for local pairs (the (e) hunk part).
- Split of the 41 red-main bugs between true semantic collisions and lint or secrets.

I filed no ddflow defects. One thing I noticed: the shell's `ls` is aliased to `exa`, which isn't installed, so plain `ls` failed throughout.</result>

## 1. What add does today (verified in code)

- **Duplicate check.** `task_add` in `[REDACTED:path]` calls `DD.check_add` (`ddflow/api/_dedupe.py`). It compares title+body only, never globs, needs or phase.
  - It lists candidates at cosine >= `show_floor` (0.35).
  - It refuses only at `ask_threshold` 0.55, and only for texts with at least `min_words` = 8 distinct words. The refusal is answered with `--new`, `--extends`, `--merge-into`, `--duplicate-of` or `--related` (`relation` over MCP). `--check` is a dry run.
  - An exact copy auto-extends. `research_task_asks=false` means a task against a research note or decision never asks.
  - The answer is stored in the `task.added` event as `dedupe {answer, score, candidates}`.
- **Phase.** `--phase`/`--parent` is optional. Only a nonexistent parent is refused (`IT.missing_parent`). There is no warning for a top-level task, and the `plan lint` findings do not include one.
- **Needs and conflicts.** Nothing at add time. `core/autoorder.py` only reacts to a lease-wait cycle (deadlock). `[schedule].auto_order` defaults to `propose`, and it was applied 0 times in the log.
- **Globs.** The MCP description of `task_add` says "ALWAYS set globs". Nothing enforces it.
- **Waves.** `[waves].auto_stamp` (default true, `api/waves_auto.py`) restamps changed waves after any graph-changing command. It landed on main 2026-10-29 (commit 70120e76a). In this worktree `declared/waves.py` is still the old stub, so I read main.
- **Priority.** DX tasks and bug fixes get `dx_priority` 8 and `bug_priority` 10 when no priority is given (`config_sections/schedule.py`).
- **Whole-queue lint.** `ddflow plan lint` (DX-queue-lint, done) finds overlap without a needs edge, duplicates, missing globs, DX/fix at priority 100, and stale needs and refs. It is on-request only and slow: `--phase P-optimizer` took 41 s here. `DX-readme-glob-diet` (open) is a hot-file budget for globs. `RR-lint` (open) builds on `plan lint`.
- **Auto-filed fix tasks.** `bug file-tasks` and `bug found` file `fix-<bug>` through `_file_fix_task` (`api/knowledge/bugs.py`). The standing `bugs`/`bugs-2` phase is reused or made, and no `check_add` runs, because the bug was already checked.
- **Command routes.** `ddflow chore` only commits chore files; it adds no tasks. `batch` and import carry no dedupe field in the log.
- **Rules about tasks.** None among the 10 project rules (`.ddflow/rules/*.toml`). The agent instructions (`templates/claude_agents/*.md`) and `CLAUDE.md` say nothing about add hygiene.
- **Shipping default rules.** `GuidanceFiles` reads shipped rules from `ddflow/templates/guidance/rules/` beneath the project's rules. That directory does not exist yet, so nothing ships today. Upgrade notes go in `ddflow/templates/upgrade/unreleased/`.

- 2,209 tasks (63%) carry a recorded answer: 2,109 `new`, 100 `related`.
- Of those, 541 scored at least 0.55 (so were refused until answered): 529 `new` and 12 `related`.
- Answers that extend or merge create no task; they show up as 44 `record.extended` events, only 14 of them on tasks (43 `extends`/`merge_into`, 1 `duplicate_of`).
- That is about 555 asks answered, with roughly 95% `--new` and 2.5% extend or merge.
- 1,668 tasks passed `--new` below the threshold, unprompted. 451 of those had no candidate at all, so agents pass `--new` as a habit.
- 1,302 tasks (37%) have no dedupe record: 745 auto-filed fixes, 511 other, 46 DX. The "other" ones are bulk roadmap imports (`B-upgrade.1..7`, `B-rules-*`) that bypass the check.

**Duplicates that got through.**
- 68 tasks were later abandoned or removed with a duplicate-like reason (`duplicate|folded|merged into|absorb|supersed|subsumed|same as|redundant`). The regex is my own; treat it as a lower bound.
- By group: other 21 of 2,385 (0.9%), `fix-` 24 of 780 (3.1%, mostly bugs closed as duplicates), DX 23 of 346 (6.6%).
- Median time from add to abandonment is 15 h (mean 93 h, p90 332 h). 66% were abandoned within 24 h.
- 33 tasks were folded by the 2026-10-16/18 roadmap review, several DX pairs scoring only 0.19 to 0.38.
- Of the 42 dup-abandoned tasks that had a dedupe record, the real target was among the candidates for only 5. Recall is low for semantic duplicates.
- The 0.55 ask is also mostly noise: only 2 of the 529 `new` answers at 0.55 or above were later dup-abandoned.
- Dup-abandon rate by group: `new` below 0.55 was 40 of 1,668 (2.4%), tasks with no record 26 of 1,302 (2.0%).

**Dependencies.**
- Needs were empty at add and filled later for 164 tasks: DX 63 of 282 (22%), other 80 of 528 (15%), `fix-` 21 of 771 (3%).
- Globs were empty at add and filled later: `fix-` 261 of 344 (median 3 h), DX 45 of 107 (median 30 h), other 56 of 570 (median 8 h).
- Waiting for files: 455 `lease.waiting` events, 220 holder/item pairs, 201 distinct items (`fix-` 100, other 58, DX 43). Of the 220 pairs, 85 later acquired; the median wait was 20 min and the total 177 h.
- Of 373 waiter-to-blocker item pairs, only 6 (1.6%) have a needs edge in either direction. Waiting is almost entirely hot-file contention with no declared order.

**Waves.**
- Before 2026-10-29, 194 of 3,511 tasks (5.5%) had a wave tag at add; later restamps were by `coordinator` and `qa-graph`.
- After auto-stamp, 453 of 541 tasks (84%) had a wave within 10 minutes of add.
- I could not measure stale stamps from the log. `ddflow waves --check` showed none in this worktree.

**Outcomes.**

| Group | Added | Done | Gone | Open 14 days or more |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DX, no phase | 291 | 109 | 37 | 80 (27%) |
| `fix-`, no phase | 390 | 331 | 50 | 9 |
| other, no phase | 109 | 59 | 14 | 17 |
| other, with phase | 2,276 | 531 | 107 | 1,011 |

The DX "fast lane" is not fast: 27% of those tasks sat open for two weeks or more.

**Are DX and `fix-` exemptions justified?**
- `fix-`: partly. They are born from a checked bug, 85% complete, and 3.1% are dup-abandoned (mostly bug-level duplicates). They still need a globs and ordering proposal, because 76% start with no globs (344 of 390 in the no-phase group; 261 later filled) and they account for 100 of the 201 distinct items that waited.
- DX: not justified. 7x the duplicate rate, 22% late needs, 84% no phase, 27% stale.

**Latency.** `ddflow task add --check` took 12 to 16 s on this loaded machine, so a second call per add is too expensive. The proposal must ride the add itself.

## 3. External grounding

- **[V, secondary sources]** Kanban's expedite class of service is conventionally capped at a WIP limit of 1. Without the cap the lane degrades into a second priority queue ([Kanban Zone](https://kanbanzone.com/resources/kanban/classes-of-service/), [ResumeLens](https://www.resumelens.org/blog/kanban/expedite-class-when-to-use)). I found no primary text from the originator. This supports a no-phase fast lane, but only with a cap and a reason.
- **[V]** Linear separates two mechanisms. Cheap search-based suggestions appear in the issue composer, with a higher similarity bar than in Triage. Slower, more thorough semantic suggestions are a separate triage feature. The suggestion is advisory and "mark as duplicate" is a human act ([Linear docs](https://linear.app/docs/triage-intelligence)). That matches the compute-and-propose design.
- **[K, not fetched]** A definition-of-ready checklist (INVEST or Scrum style) works when the tool shows the missing fields at entry. Mandatory fields that are bypassed with a blank answer turn into noise, which is our `--new` result.

## 4. Decision analysis

| Criterion | Rule only | Feature only | Feature plus short rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Enforceability | Advisory text; breaks `r-tell-dont-discover` | Computed; knob can lock | Computed; rule explains intent |
| Agent token cost | Rule text in every brief | One block per add | Block plus about 4 lines |
| Weak models | Forgotten | Reads one block | Same |
| Noise | None | Needs tuning (see below) | Same |
| Every project | Via shipped rules | Via config default | Both |
| Org lockability | Rule scope | `strictest` on the knob | Both |

- **Forced flags.** Keep them, but fix the signal. The 0.55 ask is 95% false positive and also misses semantic duplicates. Raise recall by adding glob and id-reference evidence and show it as a hint (`warn`) rather than a refusal. Keep the refusal only for near-identical text.
- **DX/fast tasks.** Skip the interrogation, not the proposal. The block must show for them as well, and fast-lane eligibility carries a cap (Kanban lesson, with the 27% stale figure as evidence).
- **Auto-filed fix tasks.** The bug's check covers the duplicate part, so no duplicate prompt. They still get a globs and needs proposal and a wave, but with no agent prompt: apply only high-confidence edges, as `plan lint --fix` does.
- **New work.** `OPT-signals` supplies the shared overlap index and text matcher, so reuse them (`r-reuse-core`) and do not build a third copy. `OPT-dedupe-hint` becomes the claim-time half of the same signal. `SCH-review-inbox` and `PM-review-job` should call the same proposal function when a person accepts a proposal. The workflow-path merge proposals and `LK-*` conflict probe feed the same overlap evidence once they exist.

**Minimal default rule text (`r-task-add-hygiene`, shipped as `ddflow/templates/guidance/rules/r-task-add-hygiene.toml`):**
1. Before you add a task, answer the proposal block `task add` prints: duplicates, merge target, needs, phase, wave. Do not pass `--new` without reading it.
2. Prefer `merge-into` or `extends` to a new task when a candidate shares your files or goal.
3. Set `globs`; add `needs` for any listed overlap; give a phase unless the block says fast-lane eligible.
4. Tasks ddflow files itself (bug fixes, triggers, schedule jobs) get the same block applied automatically.

**Knobs (`[tasks]`):**
- `add_check = off|warn|require` (default `warn`). `require` refuses until each hint is answered or waived.
- `fast_lane_tags` (default `dx`, `bugfix`).
- `fast_lane_cap`: open phase-less fast-lane tasks per project. The cap value is a design choice, not a measurement; I suggest starting at about 20, since DX/no-phase currently has 80 open for 14 days or more.
- `propose_needs` (`off|propose|apply`, high-confidence edges only).
- `dup_hint_floor`.
- Bulk and import routes get their own value instead of a silent bypass.
- Every knob gets a `strictest` value for org locking and the usual settable layers (`r-everything-configurable`).

**Exact add-time output** (also in `data` for MCP):

```

possible duplicates: DX-gate-run-detach 0.41 (shares README.md, "gate"); ...
merge candidates: DX-gate-run-detach (open, unclaimed)  -> ddflow task add DX-x --merge-into DX-gate-run-detach   | ddflow_task_add relation=merge_into:DX-gate-run-detach
suggested needs: DX-baseline-red-auto-accept (shares ddflow/core/model.py)  -> ddflow update DX-x --needs ...  | ddflow_update id=DX-x needs=...
phase: none given; nearest P-schedule (text 0.38)  -> ddflow update DX-x --phase P-schedule
```

Each action is rendered through the one `next_actions` renderer in CLI and MCP form. `warn` files the task and prints the block. `require` refuses with the same block.

### 1d. Planning data model

**The gate model is an ordered list with no dependencies.**
- `GateDef` in `services/gates/defs.py` has `applies_when`, `needs_branch` and `requires_evidence`, but no `after`, `needs` or stage.
- `pipeline_for` and `pipelines()` return `list[str]`.
- `enforce_order` defaults to "warn". `gate record` records out of order and emits `gate.out_of_order`, which happened 2,232 times.
- `require_outcome` demands some outcome per gate before completion.
- Concurrent gate runs are physically allowed. `running.py` writes one marker per item, gate and pid. The suite lock (`suitelock`, `[ci].max_concurrent_suites=1`) serialises ci and unit_tests across items.

So the diamond today is an unnamed convention. It is "all required, any order, join at complete and merge".

**Plan data.**
- Tasks carry `needs`, `globs`, tags and `wave:N`.
- Waves are derived topological levels, written by `ddflow waves --stamp`.
- Ordering is `[bugs_first, priority, id]`.
- `OptimizerPort` (`adapters/optimizer.py`) offers `order`, `cut`, `explain`. Its `Candidate` has terms, globs and tags. Its `Verdict.what` is one of taken, held, clash, cut.
- There is no group, no gate cost and no per-task sub-DAG. A merge decision needs a new verdict type.

## Part 2 – Measurement [V]

### Method and caveats

- **Window.** I used `item.completed` events from 2026-10-03 to 11-02.
  - 1,355 items completed, of which 1,287 were tasks.
  - 1,322 task, doc and research items had a claim; 1,268 tasks had gate outcomes.
  - 1,182 had gate processes recorded before the merge.
  - 1,297 merged items got their changed files from `git diff --numstat landed_before landed_after`.
- **Process interval.** [outcome time − `elapsed_s`, outcome time], deduplicated by `review_id`.
- **Cross-check.** The gate.started to outcome pairing agrees with `elapsed_s` (median difference 0.3 s). Pairing is noisy for duplicate starts, so I used `elapsed_s`.
- **Tree identity.** `tree_sha` is a 12-character prefix plus `+clean`. It is missing for 1,804 process runs, which are excluded from same-tree analyses.
- **Phase and lane** are not in `task.added` or in the events, so "family" is the id prefix, which is a heuristic.
- **Review fixed price.** A prior estimate in `batch-gates.md` §1.2 of 426 s fixed is `review-scaling.md`'s figure.

### Time per task: claim to merge

Sample: 1,182 tasks, 3,702 h in total.

| Segment | Share | p50 | Sum |

| Gate processes (union of intervals) | 26.8% | 38.8 min | 992 h |
| Claim to first process (implement) | 22.0% | 7.5 min | 813 h |

| Gaps over 2 h (parked or overnight) | 22.1% | 0 | 819 h |
| Last process to merge | 14.7% | 1.1 min (mean 27.6) | 543 h |

- A task has a median of 4 process bursts.
- For items with no gap over 2 h (1,116 items), the shares are:
  - processes 35%
  - implement 31%

**Hours per gate.** Combined reviews are counted once.

| Gate | Hours | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| rubber_duck | 406 | 3,027 |
| critic | 346 | 2,522 |
| ci | 322 | 1,989 |

- bug_hunt: 36%.
- Gaps of 3–4 s are the median between research, rules and implement, and between bug_hunt and dedupe.

### Path variants (process-mining view)

- 1,268 tasks have 1,089 distinct full sequences.
- 408 distinct orders of first occurrence.
- The canonical order (Rs Ru Im RD CR St CI UT BH DD MG) is 312 items, 25%.
- Other orders: ci before standards 62, critic before rubber_duck 38, bug_hunt and dedupe before ci 37, and 17 items with no gates.
- Strongest directly-follows edges:
  - Ru to Im 1,153
  - Rs to Ru 1,143
  - BH to DD 1,034
  - RD(fail) to CR(fail) 1,033, median gap 274 s
  - CR(fail) to RD(fail) 630, median gap 508 s
  - CI to UT 705, median gap 51 s
- The typical failing loop is: RD fail, CR fail, fix, RD fail, CR fail, RD pass, CR pass, St, CI, UT, BH, DD, MG.

### Gate yield and redundancy

Over 1,268 tasks (item-level, any run):

| Gate | Ever failed | First-run pass |
|---|---|---|
| research, rules, implement | 0.0% | 95–99% |
| standards | 0.7% | 87% |
| bug_hunt, dedupe | 0.1% | 89.5% |
| merge | 3.6% | 95.6% |
| unit_tests | 8.4% | 73% |
| ci | 44% | 45% |
| rubber_duck, critic | 74.6% / 74.5% | 23% |

- Review "failed" means findings were raised, not that the gate is broken.
- Triage verdicts: rubber_duck 2,786 confirmed and 2,413 refuted; critic 2,337 and 2,204. About 52% of findings are confirmed.
- **Co-failure.**
  - rubber_duck and critic: phi 0.73 (847 items both, 71 and 68 only one).
  - Against ci: phi 0.13–0.18.
  - All other pairs: below 0.1.
- **Overlap of findings.** At file level 1,694 findings share a file between the two gates, against 761 and 671 unique.

**Reading.** The judgement gates are the redundancy. rubber_duck and critic mostly find the same files, but about half their findings are unique, so they are partly redundant, not duplicates.

### Rework

Runs superseded by a later run of the same gate on a changed tree. Failed review rounds are excluded because they are feedback, not waste.

| Gate | Passes invalidated by a later tree change | Hours |
|---|---|---|
| ci | 235 | 27.8 |
| unit_tests | 131 | 23.4 |
| critic | 46 | 5.7 |
| rubber_duck | 43 | 4.4 |
| Partial or passed with unknown tree, all gates | — | about 55 |
| **Total superseded non-failed** | 762 runs | 119 h |

- That is 9% of process hours.
- The cause: ci and unit_tests ran before a review fix changed the tree.

### Fork-join potential

**How reviews run today.** Of 2,499 paired rubber_duck and critic rounds (paired within 40 min):
- 1,378 (55%) sequential, 352 h of reviewer wall time
- 750 (30%) concurrent
- 371 (15%) combined

Making all sequential pairs concurrent would save at most the shorter of each pair: **142 h upper bound** (pairing error, and some pairs are different rounds). My conservative figure is about 70 h, assuming half of the sequential pairs come from one `review --gate a,b` command.

**Same-tree multi-gate groups.**
- There are 1,649 groups. The tree is identical for every gate in a group.
- Sum 601 h, observed union 491 h, ideal (maximum per gate) 376 h.
- The remaining potential is **114 h**, in 934 items.
- Agents already overlap gates by hand, which is the 18% that union removes.
- Cross-gate concurrency from `elapsed_s` is 291 h in total, of which rubber_duck with critic is 124 h.

**Final-tree diamond** (the last passing run of each gate in 1,041 items):

| Schedule | Hours |
|---|---|
| Union observed | 389 |
| Review ‖ (ci + unit_tests), suite-lock aware | 280 |
| Ideal, everything concurrent | 237 |

- Saving: **109 h** (lock aware) to **152 h** (no suite lock).
- Per item this is about 5.5–8 min.
- Against 5,490 h of claim-to-complete: 2.0–2.8%.

**Speculation risk.** Forking ci with a review round that has not converged is wasted in the 75% of items where the review changes the tree. It adds load to the single suite server (`max_concurrent_suites=1`).

### Task-merge candidates

- **Method.** Pairs of tasks claimed within 30 min of the other's merge (or overlapping in life), with source-file overlap. Generated paths are excluded: tests/golden, README, docs, upgrade templates and events templates. Pairs are greedy-disjoint, ranked by the smaller item's process time.
- **Median item** is 175 source lines; 46% are under 150 lines.
- **Conservative** is the final-pass ci plus unit_tests of the smaller member. **Optimistic** is all process time of the smaller member (failed rounds included).

| Rule | Disjoint pairs | Conservative | Optimistic | Mean combined lines |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Overlap, both <150 lines, combined <300 | 46 | 5.5 h | 22.3 h | 149 |
| Overlap, combined <400 | 101 | 13.6 h | 53.8 h | 253 |
| Overlap, combined <600 | 157 | 24.7 h | 113.8 h | 377 |
| Same family, combined <400 | 141 | 18.8 h | 72.8 h | 242 |
| Any overlap, no cap | 275 | 51.6 h | 263.5 h | 1,066 |

The uncapped line is the only large one, and it breaks the review-size limit.

**Added risk** per merge: a bigger diff to review (and per-line depth falls); lost attribution and bisect granularity; wider lease; one author for two intents.

### What the log cannot answer

- Lock-queue wait before 10-23, and reviewer queue wait.
- The time spent in standards (roborev) and in merge-stage ci (`ci.result` stage merge has no `elapsed_s`, 1,296 runs, 119 failed).
- Merge-queue wait: queue entries live in `.ddflow/local`.
- Human wait: P-observe.telemetry owns this, and `stages` already names it as not measured.
- Per-item phase and lane membership.
- Which judgement-gate records took thinking time versus a quick call.
- Whether a "sequential" review pair came from one `review --gate a,b` command or two commands.

## Part 3 – External evidence

| Idea | Source | Credible for ddflow? |
|---|---|---|
| Task clustering | [V] Chen and Deelman, "Workflow Overhead Analysis and Optimizations", WORKS 2011. [Montage: makespan −53.3% with jobs reduced from 3,461 to 104.](https://scitech.group/files/publications/chen2011overhead.pdf) Average overhead per job barely changed; cumulative overhead fell | Only as an analogy. The gain came from per-job queue overhead on a grid; ddflow has a per-task fixed review price. Credible for small pairs. A 53% claim does not transfer |
| Horizontal versus vertical clustering | [K] Pegasus, WorkflowSim. A 2011 search snippet was not enough, so I did not verify the definitions | Same-gate-across-tasks is horizontal (BG-*); same-task-sequence is vertical (the within-task merge of bookkeeping records) |
| Process mining, DFG, variants, performance DFG | [V] PM4Py documents `discover_performance_dfg` (min, max, mean, median per edge). [K] van der Aalst, Process Mining: Data Science in Action | Credible as measurement only. Implementing it as 30 lines of stdlib code is enough; do not add PM4Py |
| Value stream mapping, flow efficiency | [K/V secondary] Process time over lead time; one wiki says 5–10% | ddflow's 27% is not a worse number but a different stage definition; do not compare |
| HEFT, critical-path priority | [V] Topcuoglu, Hariri, Wu, IEEE TPDS 13(3), 2002: highest upward rank first, earliest finish time. Already planned as OPT-order-v2's critical-path rank | Credible. Merge decisions must still pass the +10% makespan guard |
| GitHub Actions `needs` | [V] A job with `needs: [job1, job2]` waits for both. If a needed job fails or is skipped, dependents are skipped unless `if: always()` | Direct model for stages and a join. Note the failure semantics: ddflow wants every outcome recorded, never skipped |
| Merge trains, speculative batching (Bors, Zuul, Uber SubmitQueue) | [K] See batch-gates.md §2, which marks these UNVERIFIED | Credible for ci across tasks (BG-ci), not for review |
| Bazel and Buck remote execution | [K] Not fetched | Out of scope: ddflow gates are not hermetic actions |
| Review size | [V] Google (Sadowski et al., ICSE-SEIP 2018): [median 24 changed lines, about 90% of changes under 10 files, median review latency under 4 hours, median 1 reviewer.](https://sback.it/publications/icse2018seip.pdf) [V secondary] SmartBear/Cisco, vendor-summarised: 200 lines is a good limit, 400 the maximum, 400–500 lines per hour | Argues against bigger tasks. ddflow's median change (175 source lines) is already about 7 times Google's |

**Hype.**
- Auto-merging tasks to cut overhead. Review depth per line falls with size (confirmed findings per kchar 0.086 to 0.006, from review-scaling).
- Speculative ci‖review forking. It wastes work on 75% of items.
- Any claim of tens of percent from the gate path alone. Measured: 2–3%.

## Part 4 – Design

### Safety rules (WP-guards)

1. **A merged gate still carries its own outcome.** It has its own note and its own evidence, written in one transaction (BG-record). Never one shared "covered" record for several gates.
2. **Automatic only for bookkeeping with identical inputs on the same tree:**
   - recording research, rules and implement together
   - recording bug_hunt and dedupe together
   - covered_by (ci covers unit_tests)
3. **Proposal-only:**
   - merging tasks
   - dropping or reordering a required gate
   - running two judgement gates as one
   - forking reviews whose reviewers differ
4. **Reviewer independence stays per item.**
5. **Attribution stays per item**, via a path to member manifest.
6. **A notice never changes what is required.** The change is recorded first, as a plan revision.
7. **Hot, security and `tier:deep` globs are never merged.** This is D-BG-Q5.

**Phase reasons.** P-gate-flow is new. The gate DAG changes completion, `verify` and `enforce_order`, which is neither perf metrics nor the optimizer, and its globs are different. The rest reuse existing phases. P-batch-gates stays the home for cross-item sharing, and WP-merge-detect-tasks is its detector, not another batcher.

**In-flight handling for the three cases.**
- "Gate X is now covered by Y": WP-plan-record writes the revision and the explicit `skipped`, then WP-plan-notice tells the agent.
- "Run these as one": a plan revision with `run_together`, plus the notice. The agent runs `gate run-set`.
- "Your task was merged into Z": LC-unite (already planned) does the work; WP-plan-notice sends the notice, and the donor's lane is freed with LC-capsule. This stays a coordinator decision.

**Acknowledgement.** The agent echoes the plan revision on its next heartbeat. After N minutes without an echo (a knob), a repeat notice goes out. P-context-sync.ack does the escalation later. Honest limit: ddflow cannot force a model to read.

### Recommended order

1. **Measure first, no behaviour change.**
   - WP-path-collect, then WP-path-variants, WP-gate-yield and WP-path-telemetry.
   - Then WP-path-effect as the baseline.
   - Almost all of this is small, and it removes the guesses in this note's "cannot answer" list.
2. **Cheap wins.**
   - WP-gate-stages (silences 2,232 warnings; an existing config does not change).
   - WP-review-fork, after DX-review-concurrent-runs.
   - WP-record-many, after BG-record.
3. **The data contract.** WP-plan-record, then WP-guards.
4. **The diamond.** WP-gate-fork on the final tree only, then WP-merge-detect-gates.
5. **Tasks and optimizer, last.** WP-merge-detect-tasks, then WP-plan-notice, then WP-opt-merge-decision. The last one needs OPT-order-v2 and OPT-simulate, and should not be started before they land.

**What I would not build.**
- Task merging as an automatic default. It is worth at most 14–54 h with a 400-line cap, and the review-size evidence is against it.
- Speculative ci‖review.
- A second process-mining dependency.

### Questions for WP-decide

1. May the research, rules, implement records and the bug_hunt, dedupe records be written in one call, each with its own note?
2. Should `[review].parallel_gates` default to on after one week of measurement?
3. What is the cap for a task merge: 300 or 400 combined lines, and are risk globs excluded?
4. Should accepted proposals auto-create a plan revision, or stay proposals the operator accepts?
5. Is forking ci with a review round that has not converged ever allowed? I recommend no.

## 2. Details per tool

### 2.1 Grok Build (harness, lane worker)

**Already in ddflow:** `ddflow/harnesses/grok.toml` is on main. It was added by DX-grok-hook-descriptor, dated 2026-10-30, and the file lists Grok Build's docs pages as its sources. It uses family label `xai-grok` and a copilot-style normalizer. Its own `unverified` list says fixtures are synthetic and nothing was recorded live. It is not in this worktree, which is behind main. P-agent-parity has a `B-ac-grok` reference. The mcpshim client row `grok-build` says "docs silent; refresh is manual".

**Facts that close gaps in that descriptor** [V]. Sources are the user guide at `github.com/xai-org/grok-build/tree/main/crates/codegen/xai-grok-pager/docs/user-guide` (files 10, 12, 14, 15, 22, 24) and docs.x.ai pages.

- **Hooks (file 10):**
  - Global hooks are `[REDACTED:path]`, always trusted. Project hooks are `<project>/.grok/hooks/*.json`, silently skipped until the folder is trusted with `/hooks-trust` or `--trust`.
  - Grok also reads `[REDACTED:path]`, `.claude/settings.json` and Cursor hook files. TOML `[[hooks.<Event>]]` is also supported.
  - Handlers are `command` or `http`. Timeout is 5 s, or 600 s for Stop, SubagentStop and PostToolUse.
  - These events can block: UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, Stop, SubagentStop. PostToolUse is read but cannot block. SessionStart and others are observe-only.
  - PreToolUse blocks with stdout JSON `decision: allow|deny|ask|defer`, or exit 2 with stderr as the reason. Other non-zero exits, timeouts and malformed output fail open.
  - Stop and SubagentStop block with `{"decision":"block","reason":...}`, which feeds the reason back. After 8 continuations in one turn the turn ends anyway.
  - `additionalContext` works on PreToolUse (delivered after the tool runs), PostToolUse and Stop. It is clipped at 10,000 characters. It is not documented for SessionStart or UserPromptSubmit, and stdout of an allowing UserPromptSubmit hook is discarded.
  - Stdin is JSON with camelCase keys: `sessionId`, `toolName`, `toolInput`, `cwd`, `workspaceRoot`, `permissionMode`. It also carries `hook_event_name` (Claude PascalCase). The environment has `GROK_SESSION_ID`, `GROK_HOOK_EVENT`, `GROK_WORKSPACE_ROOT` and `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`.
- **Instructions (file 12):** reads `AGENTS.md`, `Agents.md`, `AGENT.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, and loads every match in a directory. Deeper files win. Loading needs folder trust.
- **MCP (docs.x.ai/build/features/mcp-servers.md, via search snippet, so partly secondary):**
  - TOML `[mcp_servers.<name>]` in `[REDACTED:path]`; `grok mcp add --scope project` writes `.grok/config.toml`.
  - `.mcp.json` and `.cursor/mcp.json` are read at lower priority; `${VAR}` expands; `grok mcp doctor` diagnoses.
  - Transports and tool-count limits are not stated. Project MCP needs the same trust as hooks.
- **Headless (file 14):**
  - `grok -p`, `--prompt-file`, `--prompt-json`; `-m`, `--effort`, `--max-turns`, `--cwd`, `--rules`.
  - Sessions: `-s <uuid>` creates, `-r` resumes, `-c` continues, `--fork-session`.
  - Tool control: `--tools`, `--disallowed-tools`, `--permission-mode`, `--allow`/`--deny` patterns like `Bash(npm*)`. `--yolo` / `--always-approve` skips prompts, but deny rules and hooks still apply.
  - `--output-format` takes `plain|json|streaming-json|streaming-messages-json`. Streaming-json events are `text, thought, tool_call, tool_call_update, usage, plan, end, error`, with `end` always last.
  - **Exit codes: 0, 1, 130 (SIGINT), 143 (SIGTERM).** The descriptor listed exit codes as unverified.
  - `GROK_HOME` isolates state. `GROK_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER` and `GROK_MEMORY=0` switch off updates and memory. `XAI_API_KEY`, `grok login --device-auth` and `grok login` are the auth routes.
  - Usage fields: token counts, `total_cost_usd` (absent means unreported, not zero), `cost_is_partial`, `usage_is_incomplete`, `total_cost_usd_ticks` (1 USD = 10^10 ticks).
- **ACP (file 15):** `grok agent --always-approve stdio` speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio. The calls are `initialize`, `session/new` (takes `mcpServers`, `_meta`), `session/prompt`, `session/update`, `session/load` and `session/set_config_option`. This fits P-acp (AC-backend, AC-registry).
- **Permissions (file 22):** modes `default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions`. PreToolUse hooks run first, then `deny > ask > allow` rules. `dontAsk` is documented for strict CI allowlists. An org can lock bypass off in `/etc/grok/requirements.toml`.
- **Usage and quota (file 24):** OTel metrics (`grok_code.token.usage` by type and model) and an `api_request` event. There is no cost metric, no quota or rate-limit interface, and no usage log file. `/usage` exists in the TUI, but I did not read its output format. A quota reader for the subscription is not documented, so it stays `unavailable`.
- **Maturity and licence:** Apache-2.0 first-party code [V]. External contributions are not accepted; the repo is synced from xAI's monorepo [V]. Launch was May 2026 as an early beta [V via secondary sources]. Version 1.0.0 on 2026-08-07 is one unverified timeline [K]. A cheat sheet shows v0.2.101 on 2026-07-16 [K]. The beta was gated to SuperGrok and X Premium Plus [K, secondary].
- **Terms:** I found no ban on headless use. The docs I read do not address CI use of subscription credentials. API-key headless use (`XAI_API_KEY`) is explicitly documented. **Not verified: the xAI Terms of Service.**
- **Quirks:**
  - The project trust gate silently drops hooks and MCP in a fresh worktree. A lane needs `--trust` or a pre-written `trusted_folders.toml`, or `GROK_FOLDER_TRUST=0`. This is the same shape of trap as Pi's.
  - Grok's own `grok-cli` (superagent-ai) is a different tool.

**Fit.** Grok Build is the easiest new agent to support, because it is a near-clone of the Claude Code contract. The remaining work is a lane driver, a dedicated normalizer and a live probe.

### 2.3 Muse Code (harness, lane worker) and the Meta Model API (reviewer)

All [V] from `dev.meta.ai/docs/muse-code`, `/extending`, `/configuration`, `/subscriptions` and `/docs/pricing-rate-limits` unless marked.

- **Product:** Meta's terminal coding agent, built by Meta Superintelligence Labs. Beta on 2026-08-05 with Muse Spark 1.2 [K]. Muse Spark 1.3 shipped 2026-09-02 [K]. Whether it left beta is a single secondary claim [K]. It is **proprietary**, locked to Muse models, and has a TypeScript SDK `@muse-code/sdk` plus `muse serve` (versioned session protocol; `muse schema` prints its JSON schema).
- **Install and auth:** `curl -fsSL https://dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash`. CI auth is `META_API_KEY`, which I read from the docs; the Model API page itself says `MODEL_API_KEY`. That variable-name conflict needs a probe. Browser login also works.
- **Instructions:** reads `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.agents/AGENTS.md` and `.claude/CLAUDE.md` at each directory level up to `.git`. Loading needs workspace trust. `muse init` writes `AGENTS.md`.
- **Settings:** `[REDACTED:path]` with required `"schema_version": 1`. It holds hooks, MCP and telemetry.
- **MCP:** an `mcp_servers` block in that file.
  - `stdio` takes `command, args, env`. `streamable_http` takes `url, headers`. Both take `enabled`, and `mode` is `required` (default) or `optional`.
  - It supports `${VAR}` interpolation, `MUSE_SESSION_ID` is passed to stdio servers, `muse mcp login` handles OAuth, and `run.toolset` selects tools as `mcp__server__tool`.
  - **There is no documented project-level MCP file.** ddflow's `[mcp]` descriptor section expects a project file, so a new shape or a `settings.json` overlay is needed.
- **Hooks:**
  - `<project>/.muse/hooks.json`, plus user hooks in settings and `managed_hooks_path`. Project hooks run only after trust.
  - 17 events, including PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolBatch, PreLLMCall, PostLLMCall, PreCompact, Stop and SessionEnd. Each hook binds to one event.
  - Hooks run outside the sandbox, with a cleared environment.
  - **The stdin schema, blocking exit codes and context-injection mechanics are not documented on the page.** They need a probe. Treat the hooks style as unknown until then.
- **Skills:** `.agents/skills/<id>/SKILL.md`; it also scans `.claude/skills` and `.codex/skills`. `muse skills import --from claude` exists.
- **Subagents:** isolated git worktrees on request, default capacity 8.
- **Headless:**
  - `muse exec "<prompt>"`, `--prompt-file`, `--json` (JSONL on stdout; event schema not documented), `--max-model-steps`, `--reasoning-effort none..ultra`, `--session-id <uuid>`, `muse export --session`.
  - `--disable-approval` keeps the sandbox on. `--yolo` disables the sandbox too.
  - **Exit codes: 0, 1 (including hitting `--max-model-steps`), 2 (usage error), 130, 143.**
  - CI on Linux needs bubblewrap and a non-musl build.
- **Subscription and terms:**
  - Tiers are $5, $15, $50 and $200 a month; the Everyday tier gives 10 to 50 prompts per 5 hours. How to check remaining usage is not documented.
  - The docs state the onboarding credential "is for use with Muse Code only". The subscription therefore cannot serve as a reviewer endpoint.
  - No explicit ban on automation or CI was found, and `muse exec` is documented for CI. The docs describe the sandbox as on by default and the contributor-mode setting as applying to headless runs.
- **Privacy:** **Contributor mode** is cheaper ($0.10/$0.20 per million tokens) but allows Meta to train on content. Lanes and reviewers must pin it off (`--contributor-mode off` or `MUSE_CONTRIBUTOR_MODE`).
- **Meta Model API** (`dev.meta.ai/docs`):
  - Base `https://api.meta.ai/v1`, bearer auth. Chat Completions, Responses and Messages protocols are all served.
  - Models: `muse-spark-1.3`, `1.2`, `1.1`, `muse-wonder-1.0`, and `-contributor` variants.
  - Price per million tokens: $1.25 input, $0.15 cached input, $4.25 output; 1M context.
  - Rate limits are per team: 3,000 requests/min and 4M tokens/min. `x-ratelimit-*` headers and a 429 with `Retry-After` are provided.
  - Family: ddflow has `"llama": "meta"` but no `muse` needle, so a Muse reviewer would be an "unrecognised model", which establishes no independence. Add the needle.
- **Market relevance:** moderate and new. The $5 entry price plus Meta's reach make it plausible for single-subscription users. Muse Code is also self-reported in Herdr's agent list (`docs/ddflow/research/herdr.md`).

### 2.4 Claude Duet, dots, consumer Muse

- **Claude Duet** [V, inside.com.tw]: announced 2026-10-21, US Pro/Max waitlist, iOS/Android/web. It summarises the inbox and calendar and keeps working in the background. Approval is required before sending, paying, signing or deleting. It uses Marketplace connectors and plugins. The article mentions no API, CLI or MCP. One report says it uses Claude Code Routines [K]. The model is reported as Opus 5.5.
- **dots** [V, TechCrunch 2026-09-29]: always-on agents on GPT-6 Astra, each on its own cloud computer. They are messaged through Slack and Teams, can be given "identities, credentials, and tools through existing systems", and can launch tasks in Codex or ChatGPT. The article mentions no developer API or MCP. A Microsoft Agent 365 integration is planned.
- **Consumer Muse** [V via tech-insider]: Meta's goal-driven agent launched 2026-09-08 with no developer surface.
- **Fit.** None of these is a harness ddflow runs inside or a lane it starts. The only plausible future touchpoints are:
  - a dot using Codex, which is already a supported harness;
  - a dot with an "identity and tools" slot that could point at ddflow's MCP;
  - Duet's connectors accepting remote MCP.
  Those are watch items, not tasks to build now. Add them to the market watch (`P-agent-parity.drift`).

### 2.5 Dot (dot-coding-agent)

MIT, PyPI 0.1.0 released 2026-02-21, Python 3.12+ [V]. It has tools read/edit/write/bash/grep/find, slash commands, JSONL sessions, and loads AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md and SKILL.md. The page mentions no MCP, hooks or headless mode. It is a Pi-inspired minimal toy. Not worth a descriptor. The `P-agent-parity.wrapper` route (`ddflow run -- <cmd>`) already covers any CLI.

- **Beta churn.** Both tools are weeks to months old. Pin versions with `P-agent-parity.drift`.
- **Grok trust gate.** A lane that skips `--trust` runs without ddflow's hooks or MCP, with no error.
- **Muse sandbox gap.** MCP tools and hooks run outside Muse's sandbox. ddflow's own lease enforcement must not rely on Muse's sandbox.
- **Muse contributor mode.** Training on code is a privacy risk. Pin it off.
- **Defer:** the Muse `serve`/SDK transport, the Grok subscription quota reader, any dots/Duet integration.
- **Falsifiers:**
  - If the Grok hook payloads or `streaming-json` events differ from the docs, HX-grok-probe reopens HX-grok-facts.
  - If xAI or Meta terms forbid headless use of subscription credentials, lanes switch to API-key-only.
  - If `muse exec --json` has no stable schema, HX-muse-lane stays at stdout text plus exit codes.
  - If `hooks.json` cannot block, Muse lease enforcement falls to first-call/MCP text only.

<result># R-qa-gate: should ddflow have a QA agent as a gate?

**Recommendation.** Partly, and mostly deterministic. Add a no-LLM `evidence` gate that runs the new tests on the pre-change tree, detects weakened tests, treats a skip as not-a-pass, and reruns new tests for flakes. For high-risk globs and on a cadence it also runs a bounded mutation pass. Add an LLM QA reviewer only as an advisory lens inside the existing critic call, and have it propose mutants that ddflow executes, so the verdict is a run and not an opinion. Do not add a standalone blocking LLM QA gate: reviewers already fail 68% of items with non-converging rounds, and LLM judges are biased toward approval. Most of this is already half-built (`verify_regression_test`, the planned P-test-flows) and should extend that work, not duplicate it. The research note is filed as `R-qa-gate` (verdict CONFIRMED for the measurements; the design is THEORETICAL).

Grades: [V] means measured or fetched. [K] means from memory. Event-log figures cover 2026-10-04 to 2026-11-03 (the log spans 2026-09-28 to 2026-11-03, 131,306 events), read from the primary checkout at `[REDACTED:path]`. This worktree is 13,011 commits behind main, so I did not use it.

| research, rules, implement, dedupe | Nothing mechanical. The agent writes a note. | `tree_sha`, note |
| rubber_duck, critic | An LLM reads the diff and tries to refute it. It does not see test results. | model, chunk findings, `tree_sha` |

**Regression-test rule: the test is actually run, not just declared** [V].

## Part 3: External evidence

**Weak tests for LLM-generated fixes.**
- UTBoost (arXiv 2506.09289, ACL 2025) found test insufficiency in 23 SWE-bench Lite and 26 Verified instances, and flagged about 28.4% (170/599) of Lite and 15.7% (92/584) of Verified patches that had passed original tests. The abstract and HTML counts conflict (345 total vs 176 + 169), so cite with care [V via search snippet].
- "Are 'Solved Issues' in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly?" (arXiv 2503.15223, ICSE 2026) reports 7.8% of "correct" patches fail the developer tests, 29.6% of plausible patches behave differently from the ground truth, and a 6.2-point inflation of resolution rates. Figures differ by version [V via search snippet].
- OpenAI stopped reporting SWE-bench Verified on 2026-02-23. It audited 138 of the hardest problems and found 59.4% had material test-design or description flaws [V via search snippet; I could not fetch the page, HTTP 403].
- 2026 studies report that oracles written against faulty code mirror its behaviour, and that LLM-generated tests show a gap between coverage and mutation score: weak oracles, not low coverage, are the limit [V via search snippet; arXiv ids 2609.09315 and 2607.22880, not opened].

**Fail-before/pass-after.** SWE-bench defines FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS: a task resolves only when all F2P pass and all P2P still pass [V]. ddflow's `verify_regression_test` is this practice for bugs.

**Mutation testing.**
- Google, "Practical Mutation Testing at Scale" (arXiv 2102.11378, TSE 2021): mutating only the changed lines during code review for 24,000 or more developers on over 1,000 projects. Developers first judged 85% of surfaced mutants unproductive, so the system filters and caps mutants per line and per review [V via search snippet].
- Meta ACH (arXiv 2501.12862, FSE '25): LLMs turn issue descriptions into mutants and tests that kill them. Engineers accepted 73% of 191 reviewed tests in the test-a-thons [V]. Its own paper says some accepted tests were off-target.
- Meta TestGen-LLM (arXiv 2402.09171): 75% of generated tests built, 57% passed reliably, 25% increased coverage on the Instagram benchmark. Its filters drop any test that fails on first execution [V]. It assumes "pass = correct".
- mutmut: a full-package run takes tens of minutes, with state cached for later runs; there is no native PR-incremental mode, so a wrapper scopes it to changed files [V via search snippet]. Cost and equivalent-mutant triage are the known problems.
- PIT and cosmic-ray: [K], not checked.

**Diff coverage.** `diff-cover` reports coverage for new or modified lines from a coverage XML and supports `--fail-under` [V via search snippet].

**Hypothesis, chaos and fault injection, test-smell detectors.** [K], not checked: Hypothesis for property and stateful tests; chaos and fault injection catches resilience bugs that happy-path tests cannot; smell detectors measure assertion density and test smells but not whether a test would catch a regression.

**Flaky tests.** Google reported about 1.5% of test runs flaky and almost 16% of tests with some flakiness (Micco, Google Testing Blog, May 2016) [V via search snippet].

**LLM-as-judge reliability.** "Beyond Consensus" (arXiv 2510.11822) reports judges accept valid outputs (true-positive rate above 96%) but reject invalid ones poorly (true-negative rate below 25%), on 366 buggy Python programs [V via snippet]. "Bias in the Loop" (arXiv 2604.16790) finds verdicts shift with prompt cues for code generation, repair and test generation [V via snippet]. Judge accuracy therefore needs calibration against labelled bad tests.

**AI QA/review agents in products.**
- Cursor Bugbot: about 70–80% of its flags are resolved before merge. Self-reported and not precision or recall [V via snippet].
- Anthropic's code-review plugin: parallel agents with confidence scoring, posting issues at 80 or above, per a mirrored README [V via snippet].
- Benchmarks: vendor-run, and they disagree. CodeRabbit reports 51.2% F1 on Martian (its own write-up). GitHub's ReviewBench is open but run by an interested party. One vendor test puts Copilot at 20% precision [V via snippet]. Treat all as hype until independently replicated.
- All of these review a diff. None of them runs a fail-before check or a mutation run on your tests. Qodo and Devin are [K] only; I did not check their claims.

## Part 4: Design and recommendation

### Options

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| (1) Deterministic evidence gate | Yes, first. Extends machinery that already exists. |
| (2) LLM QA reviewer as a gate | No as a blocking gate. 68% of items already fail a review round, review is about 795 h of wall-clock, and judges lean toward approval. |
| (3) Both, staged | Yes: (1) now; the LLM only as an advisory lens and mutant proposer, after (1) exists. |
| (4) Neither | No. The measured gaps are real: unverified fixes, no check for ordinary tasks, test-quality-blind reviewers. |

### First version: cheapest, highest value

**A. `evidence` gate (command gate, no LLM), after `unit_tests`, applies to tasks.** On the item's base with the new or changed test files overlaid, it runs only the added or changed test ids:
- It records failed-before, passed-before, error kind (assertion vs import) and skipped.
- Verdict is warn (default) when the item changes source, is not tagged refactor, and no new test fails before.
- Skip, xfail and not-collected are never counted as a pass. This is `regression_run.py`.
- It reruns the new tests 3 times on HEAD (flake check), writing `flakes.jsonl`.
- The AST weakening detector reports net-removed tests, lowered assert counts, new skip/xfail, loosened numeric tolerances and updated snapshots. `D-test-flows` already sets this to warn by default, with block as a setting.
- It requires the new tests to pass at HEAD, taken from the existing unit_tests evidence, to separate "fails because of the environment" from "fails because of the missing change".

**B. Bug fixes.** F2P already exists. Remaining gaps are `could-not-run` and `overridden` (about 17–19% recently), and fixes confined to a test file. For the latter, require the existing `mutation` argument or a stability record instead of a free-text override.

**C. High-risk globs and the cadence only.** A bounded mutation pass on changed lines: at most N mutants (for example 20) and T seconds (for example 300), using the `{file, old, new}` format that `gate verify` already uses and the pass that produced `U4-weak-tests`. Survivors are recorded, never blocking. Accept equivalent mutants by id. Risk tiers come from `D-gate-economy-r3 (b)` (security, engine, hook and lease globs, tier:deep). It also replaces the `mutation_tests` cadence, which was skipped 3 of 5 times for lack of a tool.

**D. LLM lens (advisory, no extra round).**
- Feed the `evidence` gate's anomalies into the existing critic's `context`.
- Add a short test-quality `extra_rules` text. Migrate to `B-pi-review-lens` and `TF-lens` when they land.
- Optionally let it propose up to 5 mutants for the changed lines (ACH-style). ddflow runs them against the selected tests, and a surviving mutant is the finding. A finding must cite a probe.
- Independence tier follows `D-reviewer-independence-soft`. Because all models may be one family (`D-reviewer-independence-soft-why`), the deterministic parts matter most.

**Optional, needs operator consent:** diff coverage via coverage.py/diff-cover (no coverage tool is installed; install nothing unasked). Report only, no absolute threshold (Goodhart).

### What stays out
- No standalone blocking LLM QA gate and no new review round.
- No full-suite mutation per task.
- No coverage percentage threshold.
- No auto-repair of tests (`P-review-quality` rejected a second test generator).
- No use of baseline-red acceptance for `evidence` failures. `DX-baseline-red-env-isolation` is the guard against branch leakage into the base run.
- No occupation of the suite lock. The evidence run covers at most about 8 test ids, with `-n0` and a short timeout.

### Which tasks need it
- All code tasks get A, because the cost is small.
- Bug fixes get B.
- Risk-glob and tier:deep tasks get C.
- Doc-only and test-only tasks skip F2P but still get the weakening check.

### Cost
- Per task: one scratch checkout plus a pytest run of at most 8 test ids. Measured F2P runs took 1–33 s per test, with `test_scenario` at about 150 s, on a loaded host.
- Current per-item gate time is about 30 minutes (two reviews at about 6 minutes, ci about 7 minutes, unit_tests about 11 minutes).
- Estimated added cost is 1–3% of gate time. This is an estimate, not a measurement.
- No additional LLM round.
- Mutation is the one real cost, kept to risk globs and cadence with a hard budget.

### Interactions
- **tree_sha:** evidence is stamped with `tree_sha` and becomes stale when the tree changes, like other gates.
- **ci_scope / selected tests:** new tests are always in the selected set. The evidence gate may reuse `covered_by` for the HEAD pass. Selection recall escapes (`B0e7199ff32`, the Oct 18 red-main cluster) are a separate issue; a selection-audit cadence could use the same pre-change run.
- **P-batch-gates:** evidence is per item and does not need a batch run. If items are batched, results fan out per item.
- **PM-test-durations, PM-flaky:** the gate emits elapsed time and rerun results for them to consume.
- **DX-gate-auto-record-mechanical:** build beside it. Make bug_hunt's pass cite the `evidence` result. Do not retire dedupe or bug_hunt yet (0.1% yield); decide after the evidence gate has data.

### Proposed tasks (new phase `P-qa-evidence`)

Reason for a new phase: the P-test-flows chain is blocked behind `SE-event-registry`, `B-pi-scenario-run` and `P-unify`-gated work, and it targets test kinds, not the gate. The QA tasks mark `extends` against TF-* ids (not duplicates) so TF-filters, TF-mutation, TF-readonly and TF-lens later build on them. Per lesson `L-needs-on-decide-tasks`, `QA-decide` is not in any `needs`.

Wave placement: Waves 1–3 follow only the done items `DX-baseline-red-auto-accept`, `SE-eval-harness` and `B-uni-kind-pipeline`. They avoid the open P-test-flows chain. Wave 0 may start at once. Wave 4 follows QA-eval.

That is 14 tasks, all QA-prefixed, with no dependency loops. They touch `services/gates/*`, the same area as the bug-fix lanes currently queued on `api/review/**` and `services/review/**`, so expect lease waits.

### Decision questions for the operator

1. **Scope.** Run the cheap checks (pre-change run, weakening, flake rerun) on every code task? Default: yes, warn only. Mutation only on risk globs and the cadence.
2. **Warn or block.** Default: warn for the first month. Switch each check to block only after QA-eval shows a false-positive rate you accept (matches `D-test-flows (3)`).
3. **Role of the LLM.** Default: advisory lens inside the critic plus LLM-proposed mutants that ddflow executes. No standalone blocking LLM QA gate and no extra round.
4. **Tooling.** May I propose adding coverage.py/pytest-cov as a dev dependency for diff coverage, and mutmut? Default: yes to coverage.py, report-only. No to mutmut at first (use the bounded in-house mutator). Nothing is installed without your word.
5. **Placement.** New phase `P-qa-evidence` that TF-* later extends, or fold into `P-test-flows`? Default: new phase, because P-test-flows is blocked behind the `P-unify` chain.
6. **Zero-yield gates.** Should bug_hunt and dedupe (0.1% fail rate, note-only passes) be derived from machine output (`DX-gate-auto-record-mechanical`) instead of agent notes? Default: yes, but revisit retiring them after the evidence gate has a month of data.

- I ran 19 of the 40 requested revert merges and 25 of the requested 20-plus F2P runs. The rest were stopped for time under heavy host load.
- Failure-type and revert-oracle results are indicative, not statistical.
- The window has no `introduced_by` field, so the post-merge rate is a lower bound.
- External claims marked "via search snippet" were not read from the papers. The OpenAI page returned 403.
- Scratch worktrees are removed. The repository working tree was not edited. The only write was the `R-qa-gate` research event.
