<result># Agent parity and operations: what exists, what is planned, what is missing

Research note: **R-agent-parity-ops** (CONFIRMED, recorded).

I read from the main checkout `[REDACTED:path]`, because my worktree was behind main (it lacked `core/govern.py` and the v2 descriptor code). `[V]` means I ran or read it. `[K]` means documented or planned only.

## 1. What we have

### Parity matrix, 24 descriptors

I scanned the TOML sections of every descriptor in `ddflow/harnesses/*.toml` `[V]`. `ddflow harness list` shows 24 agents: it includes grok, and the 23 descriptor files plus grok's make 24.

| Capability | Coverage `[V]` |
|---|---|
| `[mcp]` | all 24, but `ddflow harness list` shows `mcp=none` for aider, cline, windsurf, replit, openhands, goose and cody |
| `[hooks]` | 18 of 24. Missing: cody, glm, qodo, replit, and (from the CLI list) aider has none, kimi lacks events |
| `[subagents]` dir | 13 of 24 |
| `[skills]` dir | 16 of 24 |
| `[plugin]` | 12 of 24 |
| `[commands]` | 11 of 24 |
| `[worktrees]` | 8 of 24 |
| `[detect]`, `[headless]`, `[autonomy]` | **grok only** |
| `[continuation]`, `[meters]`, `[caps]`, `[telemetry]`, `[spawn]`, `[acp]` | **none**, in any descriptor |

- `P-agent-parity.descriptor-v2` is marked done. It merged the schema and the strict loader, but not the data. 22 agents have nothing a launcher, governor or quota meter could read.
- `ddflow harness facts` lists 354 lines, and the 332 fact rows are all `unverified`. Only grok has `[facts.*]` entries with `documented` status, dated 2026-10-30.
- Hooks as wired today: `ddflow harness show claude` reports `prompt: declared, not delivering` and `post_tool`, `stop`, `session_end` as `wired, not injected`. Only `session_start` and `pre_tool` are native hooks.
- Headless, quota-meter and token-count parity rows are therefore `[K]` everywhere except grok headless.
- Review parity: reviewer independence rests on `[agent].families`, a substring map of model name to family (`config_sections/agent.py`). The map covers about 22 families (qwen, claude, gpt, gemini, llama, deepseek, grok, kimi, glm and others). Routers such as Copilot's HydraFusion are handled as family sets. `[V]`
- Lanes: `services/lanes/` has launch, launch_template, capacity, ledger and advise, plus opencode as the first concrete lane. These are `SW-*` tasks, done 2026-10-30 and 2026-10-31. `[V]`
- Swarm scheduler scoring (`SW-score`) and the quality ledger (`SW-ledger`) are done. Pull dispatch (`SW-pull`), headroom, hedging, reassignment and remote lanes are open.
- Subagent definitions: only 3 shipped templates, `ddflow-implementer`, `ddflow-researcher` and `ddflow-reviewer` in `ddflow/templates/claude_agents/`. No registry, versioning or sync exists. All of `B-sub-*` is open.

### Cost, quota and subscriptions

- `services/quota.py` has per-subject profiles. A subject is `agent:<harness>/<account>` or `llm:<url>`. Windows are 5h, day, week, month or total, in tokens, usd, sessions or percent. Profiles are user-level, so every project on the machine shares them. `B-quota-profiles` is done. `[V]`
- That is the whole of it. There is no `ddflow quota` or `ddflow usage` command (both are invalid CLI choices). Meters (`B-quota-meters`), pause at 80% (`B-quota-pause`, `B-quota-loop`), discovery and surfaces are all open. `[V]`
- `cost_usd` appears only in `services/swarm_metrics.py`, and `R2fa84ecdfa` records "cost_usd absent from all events". There is no ledger of spend, so the "expenses" goal has no data source today.
- Governor: `core/govern.py` is a pure `decide()` function. Quota marks are 0.4/0.6/0.8, context marks 0.6/0.75/0.85/0.95. It has tier and effort caps, reviewer and deep floors, and hysteresis. Nothing feeds it real meters yet. Its sampling, routing, surfaces and acceptance tasks are open.
- Per provider: only Claude Code has a documented vendor percent-and-reset meter (the design comment in `quota.py` says so). Everything else is `unavailable` or token counts. The grok meters task, `HX-grok-meters`, and `HX-muse-meters` are open.

### Complexity to model, effort and back pressure today

- A task's model hint is the advisory tag `tier:fast|balanced|deep` (`core/tier.py`). The tier never reaches gates or scheduling.
- Two other things are easily mistaken for complexity handling, and neither is:
  - `services/complexity_budget.py` is radon cyclomatic complexity of code, as a commit warning.
  - `B-sched-backpressure` is the schedule-side open cap for scheduled jobs.
- Governor ladders downshift by quota and context fraction, not by task difficulty. Predicting a tier per task (`tier-suggest`, `tier-heuristic`, `tier-feedback`) is open.
- Flow control (`core/flowcontrol.py`, D-adaptive-flow-accepted) gives parallelism back pressure from machine load: start 4, floor 2, ceiling 8. `P-agent-caps` adds per-agent caps with expiring slots.

### Periodic reviews, `ddflow cadence` today

The live `ddflow cadence` output lists these `[V]`:

- Count passes: integration_tests (every 5 tasks), dedupe_sweep (every 4 tasks), architecture_review (every 2 phases), mutation_tests (every 3 phases), lessons_pass (every 4 phases).
- Calendar entries through `[cadence].every_days`, such as `roadmap_review`.
- `health_watch` every 900 s.

Right now all of these are DUE, and `integration_tests` is 1485 tasks overdue. The cadence only reports that a pass is due. It runs nothing, which is the gap `P-schedule.executor-basic` covers.

### Multi-project and external swarm

- **One server, one repo** is stated in the README (line 3831): "No — one server process serves one repository." A test asserts that no tool takes a repo argument. `[V]`
- The MCP server's identity per call (`as_agent`, D-mcp-identity-per-call) already lets a foreign orchestrator's agents share one server.
- Quota profiles are the only user-level, cross-project store. The organisation knowledge hub (`P-knowledge-hub`) and the constellation phases cover cross-project sharing, but not one server hosting several repos.

## 2. What is planned (existing ids, to avoid duplicates)

| Goal | Existing ids |
|---|---|
| Parity data, launcher, continuation | `P-agent-parity.launcher`, `.continuation`, `.meters`, `.suite`, `.drift`, `.wrapper`, `.permissions`, `.new-descriptors`, `.corrections`, `.docs`; `P-agent-lifecycle.*`; `P-agent-compat` (B-ac-smoke, B-ac-fixtures, B-ac-report, B-ac-mcp-tests); the `*-fit` phases (grok, muse, pidev, dsh) |
| Token features per agent | `ATF-*`: ATF-descriptor-fields, ATF-usage-fields, ATF-quota-query, ATF-spend-caps, ATF-limit-signals, ATF-resume, ATF-terms-gate |
| Token economy | `TE-*`: TE-limit-aware-routing (layered price and limit table), TE-auto-resume, TE-spend-resume, TE-model-routing, TE-measure (done) |
| Expense ledger | `B-gap-spend` (usage ledger, UNAVAILABLE not zero), `GV-step-cost`, `GV-regret`, `FL-scorecard`, `EXT-estimates-workload` |
| Quotas | `BL-quotas` (7 tasks, 1 done); `LS-budget-per-agent` is done and covers the context budget |
| Routing and back pressure | `P-governor.*` and `GV-*`: GV-preset, GV-roles, GV-escalate, GV-capabilities, GV-harness-routers; `P-agent-caps`; `P-optimizer` (OPT-*) |
| Swarm, orchestrating | `P-swarm`: SW-pull, SW-headroom, SW-hedge, SW-reassign, SW-remote-*, SW-lead-link, SW-pilot-* |
| Swarm, as a participant | `FL-tracker-contract` (a contract an external orchestrator can drive ddflow through), `AG-a2a` (A2A lane backend and Agent Card), `DX-uc-workflow-run-ledger`, `P-remote`, `P-spawn`, the P-fleet `FL-*` tasks |
| Agent definitions | `P-subagents` (`B-sub-model`, `-events`, `-sync`, `-route`, `-sod`, `-doctor`, `-trust`, `-metrics`, `-eval`, `-defaults`, `-onboard`, `-docs`), `FL-subagent-sync`, `B-org-kinds-skills-subagents`, `B-sub-mcp-guard` |
| Stack and tool recommendation | `P-toolkit` (TK-detect, TK-catalog, TK-propose, TK-precommit-stacks, TK-dep-bot, TK-sarif, TK-gitleaks-baseline, TK-agent-research, TK-decide, TK-knobs, TK-docs, TK-ci-parity, TK-agent-hazards), all open |
| Periodic reviews | `P-schedule` (library, watch, chain, outcomes, manage, executor-basic, unattended, ddflow-set, plus `SCH-project-review`, `SCH-review-inbox`, `SCH-dep-upgrades`, `SCH-restart-survival`, `SCH-knobs`); `P-security-gate` (SEC-cadence, SEC-deps, SEC-scanners); `P-observe` and `P-autopilot` (AP-observe); `P-perf-metrics` (WP-merge-propose); `B-sched-defaults` |
| Multi-user and multi-clone | `P-multiuser`, `P-constellation(-ops)`, `P-org-config`, `P-knowledge-hub` |

## 3. Gaps against the goal list

1. **Descriptor data is the real blocker.** Schema v2 is done, but 22 of 24 agents have no `[headless]`, `[meters]`, `[caps]` or `[continuation]` data. `.launcher`, `.meters`, the governor, quota meters and the swarm all consume that data. No task owns populating it per agent, except per-agent ATF descriptor tasks for five agents (copilot, antigravity, qwen, kiro, zed, junie, continue) and the grok and kimi suites.
2. **No enforcing parity test.** `P-agent-parity.suite` is open. Nothing fails when a descriptor lacks a required capability section or a still-`unverified` fact.
3. **ddflow as a member of an external swarm.**
   - Claude Code agent teams share a task list. Task claiming uses file locking, and `TaskCreated`, `TaskCompleted` and `TeammateIdle` hooks can block with exit 2. `[V]` (official docs, fetched 2026-11-03)
   - The team's own task list lives under `[REDACTED:path]` and is session-scoped. Teammates load the same MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, so ddflow's MCP tools are reachable by every teammate.
   - No ddflow task maps those hooks to ddflow leases and gates. The only grep hits are in the swarm research doc and event logs, with no implementation.
   - Missing: a documented "participant mode" with a mapping from the foreign task list to ddflow items, a per-call `as_agent` convention for foreign teammates, and a lease and gate check on `TaskCompleted`.
4. **Multi-project in one server.** Explicitly unsupported. A user-level project registry, a cross-project roll-up of quota, spend and queue, and per-project isolation are absent. The one-server-per-repo rule is a tested invariant, so any change needs a decision first.
5. **Agent-definition lifecycle.** The registry, sync, lint, trust and eval are planned, but nothing covers create, version, test (a routing eval is `B-sub-eval`), or retire with a deprecation record. `P-deprecation` exists and could be reused.
6. **Expense and subscription accounting.** Quota profiles are declared but never metered. There is no price table, no per-event token and cost record, and nothing that aggregates one subscription across several agents (for example, Codex shares one pool across CLI, IDE and cloud). `B-gap-spend`, `TE-limit-aware-routing` and `B-quota-meters` all depend on descriptor `[meters]` data (gap 1).
7. **Complexity-based back pressure.** The tier hint is advisory and no complexity score exists. The per-task predictors (`tier-suggest`, `tier-heuristic`) are open and not tied to back pressure. What is missing is a single complexity signal (files, globs, needs, history, review rounds) that sets tier, effort, review depth and a concurrency cost weight, and tells a swarm how many simultaneous heavy tasks it may run.
8. **Stack and tool recommendation.** `P-toolkit` is all open. The toolkit has no link to the stack-aware, agent-parity side: which linters, scanners and test tools exist per language, and which of the 24 agents can run them.
9. **Periodic review catalog is incomplete.** Only five count passes and two calendar entries ship, and the cadence only reports. Missing as default jobs: bug audit, security review, dependency and upgrade review, feature and consistency review (docs vs code vs descriptors), and the parity-matrix review itself. Their outputs must be proposals, not changes. `SCH-review-inbox` and `SCH-project-review` cover the inbox and one combined review. No catalog defines each review's cadence, runner, output form and dedupe rule.

### Review catalog, proposed

| Review | Cadence | Runner | Output | Dedupe | Exists? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bug audit | weekly | executor, cross-family agent | proposal records | against open bugs/tasks | `B-sched-defaults` (open) |
| security | weekly + on risky diffs | `SEC-*` | findings to bugs | `SEC-findings` | planned |
| architecture | every 2 phases | agent | proposals | open tasks | cadence entry only |
| code quality / duplication | every 4 tasks | `dedupe_sweep` | proposals | existing | cadence entry only |
| dependency / upgrade | weekly | `SCH-dep-upgrades`, `TK-dep-bot` | branch, never auto-merged | open tasks | planned |
| feature / roadmap | 7 days | `roadmap_review` | proposals | open tasks | calendar entry |
| consistency (docs, descriptors, parity) | monthly | `docs check`, parity suite | report | existing bugs | missing |
| agent-definition drift | monthly | `B-sub-doctor` | report | existing | planned |
| cost and quota | weekly | metrics | digest | none | missing |

## 4. Best practices and other tools

Date-sensitive items are marked.

- **Claude Code agent teams** (docs fetched 2026-11-03, `[V]`): experimental, enabled by `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`; one team per session, no nested teams, no resume of in-process teammates.
  - Task states are pending, in progress and completed, with dependencies.
  - Teammates inherit the lead's permission mode, and teammates cannot approve each other's permission prompts or supply consent for the operator. That matches ddflow's "no agent consent" rule.
  - A teammate's model is chosen in order: spawn prompt, definition `model`, `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`, the lead's model.
  - The docs warn that teams cost significantly more tokens, and say to prefer subagents for sequential or same-file work. That supports tying team size to task complexity.
- **GitHub Agent HQ** (secondary sources, `[unverified]` against GitHub docs): Claude and Codex in public preview for Copilot Pro+ and Enterprise. One premium request per agent session, plus central policy and audit logging. This confirms "which agents and models are permitted" as an org-level policy, which `P-org-config` can carry.
- **LiteLLM** (`[V]` via docs search): virtual keys with per-key, user and team budgets, TPM/RPM limits, model allowlists, fallbacks, and a budget fallback that reroutes to another model. Needs Postgres for spend tracking. Per-model and tag budgets may be Enterprise-only (`[unverified]`). **OpenRouter**: per-key credit limit with daily, weekly or monthly reset, and a `/key` endpoint reporting remaining credit and usage. Both support ddflow reading remaining budget from an HTTP route instead of guessing, which fits the `ATF-quota-query` shape. Do not build a proxy.
- **Codex** (secondary sources, `[unverified]`, date-sensitive): usage is bundled into ChatGPT plans, with a rolling 5-hour window shared across CLI, IDE and cloud plus a weekly cap. One source says OpenAI temporarily removed the 5-hour limit in July 2026. Check before relying on it.
- **LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen** (`[V]` from secondary comparisons only): LangGraph has the strongest checkpoint persistence. CrewAI is role-based. AutoGen is in maintenance, with AG2 as the community fork and Microsoft Agent Framework as successor. I found nothing on MCP support or interrupt mechanics, so those are `[unverified]`. The lesson to take is checkpointing plus human-in-the-loop interrupts, which ddflow already has through events, leases and approvals.
- **Renovate, Dependabot, OpenSSF Scorecard**: Scorecard's dependency-update check only tests that Renovate or Dependabot is configured, and running both can duplicate PRs. Renovate supports `minimumReleaseAge` (the docs show "3 days"). Dependabot cooldown, Semgrep SARIF and SonarQube were not verified. Conductor, OpenHands and Codex-vs-Copilot HQ details were not researched either.

data.text:
Check what are the capabilities of ddflow for observability, best practices, benefits as part of our logs, and statistics we collect, for ddflow as a tool and so, and for the auto optimization process, but also in parallel - ddflow to observe, monitor and react or manage development of observability features on per project basis. See best practices, what is applicable for our tool, and what what we can do, what we plan to do, what makes sense, where we have gaps and propose features and implementation phase for the gaps you find. Check this paper on the topic too but critically as it might have irrelevant ideas

Observability helps teams monitor when things go wrong and profile how things change over time; basically, knowing what’s going on under the hood in your app. This post will go through:

What observability actually is, and the logs and metrics your app emits to tell you what the hell is going on.
How to use that data when something breaks, from figuring out where the problem is to getting the app back online.
How to catch problems before your users do, with monitoring, alerting, and, when you’re feeling fancy, automated action.
Let us dive in, keen observers.

Previously, at Vandelay Industries

To recap, Art Vandelay is vibe coding the app that runs Vandelay Industries’ potato chip import/export empire, or as we know it in the Godfather, the family business. And never ask me about my business.

Jason Alexander, who played George Costanza, in a navy New York Yankees x Kith varsity jacket, sitting on a stool holding a paper coffee cup.
So far in this series, we’ve explained every piece of how Art gets to a working app:

In Part 1 we split it into a frontend and a backend.
Part 2 gave it a place to store data: a Postgres database on Railway.
Part 3 locked the doors by adding in auth (so that Newman can’t read the shipping schedule).
Part 4 put it in the cloud and gave it a real public URL so users can actually access it.
Part 5 scaled it up to accommodate additional traffic after it went more or less viral.
So Part 5 got your app back from the brink of the dreaded “500 server error”, and in the process we learned about scaling: horizontal for more copies of your app, and vertical for beefier servers. We also learned how to ensure your app scales up to accommodate load, and then back down automatically, keeping things snappy without overspending. It’s nice when things work automatically, but some day, you’ll need to know what’s actually going on under the hood.

So after scaling up/out, Art was able to get his app back online; but now he’s scared. He might have fixed this problem, but he has no visibility into what the next problem is going to be, i.e. what’s happening: who is accessing it, how close his servers are to overloading, or if a giant bot farm is DDOSing him (well maybe that’s just paranoia). Last time, he only learned his site was down when Elaine helpfully notified him that she couldn’t get in.

It’s imperative, for the continued success of Vandelay Industries, that Art finds out about issues with the import/export app before his users do. He needs to put some damn guardrails in place. To understand how to do this, let us first dive into some basics about observability.

Observability 101

A system is said to be observable if a maintainer of that system can understand its internal state without access to it, or said differently, using only data emitted from the system. **yawn**

Nah but for real. A system (Art’s app in this case) needs to continuously publish data that tells him what the hell is going on. That way, when something goes wrong, he can check that data to get an understanding of what went wrong and how he might go about fixing it. It’s like a black box in an airplane, but with much much higher stakes. This data takes many forms, but a few of the most common are logs and metrics.

Logs

Logs are a record of things that happened inside your system. updated user account, attempting to connect to database, compiled code into binary. That sort of thing.

For Art’s app, a useful log might look something like:

ERROR: Failed to create shipment: database connection refused
​
That’s much, much, more useful than Elaine calling and saying, “the import thingy doesn’t work.” Now Art knows he has a database problem and can go troubleshoot it.

A log can really take any form; it’s just a bunch of text. There are a few different kinds of logs worth knowing about:

Build logs tell you what happened while your platform was turning your code into something it could run. If you referenced a software package that doesn’t exist, or your build system had trouble packaging up your app, the answer is probably here.
Runtime/application logs are emitted while your app is actually running. This is where anything you choose to log in code, such as warnings, errors, database connection failures, and other application events show up.
Request and network logs tell you about traffic moving into, out of, and around your application: requests arriving, status codes being returned, network connections failing, and so on.
As a developer you can infinitely customize what kinds of logs you want to capture and how they’re structured. As a vibe coder…you are probably safe with whatever your deployment platform of choice defaults to.

On Railway, Art’s platform of choice, logs are captured and surfaced in the dashboard automatically. Not only this, but they’re fully searchable and filterable by severity and type.

Railway's Observability log view for a production environment: a table of timestamped log lines from Frontend and Backend services, one expanded to show its service, deployment and replica ids, with a column picker open on the right.
The important thing to know is that logs give you specific events to investigate. If Art knows his app stopped working at 2:17 PM, he can pull up the logs from around 2:17 and start looking for something suspicious. Something like:

ERROR creating shipment 1842: database connection timed out
​
That gives Art a place to start; at least a section of the haystack in which to look for the pesky needle jamming up his app.

Metrics

If logs are broadly qualitative, metrics are their nerdy quant cousin. They are structured representations of measurements taken repeatedly over time.

Instead of telling you that one particular thing happened, they tell you how dimensions of your system are behaving in aggregate:

CPU usage is at 92%.
Memory consumption has doubled over the last hour.
Network traffic is suddenly five times higher than usual.
Disk usage is slowly approaching its limit.
These are metrics. Some of the most useful infrastructure metrics are:

CPU usage: how much work your server’s processor is doing relative to how much work it has the capacity to do.
Memory usage: how much of your allotted RAM your application is consuming.
Disk usage: how much persistent storage you’re using.
Network traffic: how much data is moving into and out of your services.
Railway collects these resource metrics for services automatically and exposes them as easy to read graphs.

Railway's Metrics tab for a service called Docs Frontend over seven days: a CPU chart with occasional small spikes, and a Memory chart climbing repeatedly toward a 4 GB line, dropping at each deploy and climbing again.
Metrics become particularly useful because you can look at them over time. Seeing that your app is using 700 MB of memory right now may not mean much. Seeing that it used 200 MB yesterday, 400 MB this morning, and 700 MB now tells you something is probably wrong.

So commit this to memory, young vibesmith: Logs tell you what happened, thing by thing. Metrics tell you what’s happening to the system, all at once.

The two are most powerful when used together. Suppose Art gets reports that the app became painfully slow around noon. His metrics show CPU usage shooting to 100% at 11:58 (you do not want your CPU to be at 100%). He then checks the logs from the same time and discovers thousands of requests hammering the shipment-search endpoint.

Now he’s able to evolve from “the app is slow” to “this endpoint is overwhelming the server” and something is wrong with shipment search.

That, my friends, is observability.

Technically helps you make practical sense of software + AI, once a week.

Upgrade to paid
Using Observability Data

So what do we do once our app is observable? There are two times people really tap into observability data: during an incident, and to prevent an incident. The more you do the latter, the less you have to do the former. Art’s platform of choice, Railway, comes stock with a number of observability features we’ll explore throughout.

A Railway Observability dashboard for a project: usage cost tiles (current usage $359.16, estimated $425.54), Frontend CPU and Database CPU charts, a live All Logs panel, and Database Memory and Service Memory charts over the last day.
A beginner’s guide to incident management

When something goes horribly wrong in your app – people see the wrong data, users can’t check out, the app goes down altogether, or anything prevents a user from using a substantial or critical portion of your app – congratulations, you have an incident on your hands. It’s a rite of passage, really, and you should take a moment to congratulate yourself. Then you should crack a caffeinated beverage and lock the hell in, cause your uptime is on the line.

The first job during an incident is to figure out where the issue is actually occurring. “The app is down” is not, unfortunately, a particularly useful diagnosis. Maybe the newest version of the app never built successfully. Maybe it built and deployed, but crashes as soon as it starts. Perhaps the app is perfectly healthy but can’t connect to Postgres, or one particular endpoint is throwing errors, or everything technically works but takes 45 seconds to load. We have a bunch of possible culprits, so the point of all that observability data we just talked about is to narrow the field.

A good place to start is with whatever changed most recently. If Art deployed a new version of the app at 2:03 and Vandelay Industries ceased to function at 2:04, this is not a Sherlock level mystery; something in the new version is borked. Railway keeps the history of your deployments, so Art can see pretty quickly whether the timing lines up, and rollback (revert to a previous version) if necessary.

Railway's Deployments tab for vandelay-industries-import-manager, showing its public railway.app URL and an active deployment, 'Updating node version', pushed via GitHub two minutes ago and marked Deployment successful.
If the deployment itself failed, the build logs are the next place to look. Applications have to be turned from source code into something that can actually run, and the build logs record that process. Maybe a dependency wouldn’t install, some code wouldn’t compile, or the AI hallucinated a potato-chip-sdk package with the sort of confidence normally reserved for packages that ya know, actually exist. If the app never finished building, there’s no point investigating what it did after it started, because it never did.

A failed Railway deployment: Initialization passed, Build image failed after 12 seconds with 'Failed to build an image. Please check the build logs for more details.', and the Deploy and Post-deploy steps marked Not started.
If the build worked, then we move on to the logs from the running application. This is where Art will see the app starting, connecting to the database, handling requests, and, crucially, throwing logs when one of those things goes wrong. An error like database connection timed out gives us a substantially better idea of what’s happening than “Elaine says it’s broken.”

Railway lets you search and filter logs, so rather than reading every line the app has ever emitted, start around the time the incident began and look for obvious suspects: errors, failed connections, timeouts, or messages from whatever part of the app users are having trouble with.

Railway's Observability log view again: timestamped log lines from Frontend and Backend services, searchable with a filter bar along the top.
It can also be useful to look directly at the requests hitting the app from the internet. Every time your browser asks the backend for something, that request is resolved with an HTTP status code, and those codes provide a wonderfully terse assessment of how things went.

200 means, broadly, everything is fine.
A 400-something response generally means there’s a problem with the request, authentication, permissions, or something else on the client side.
A 500-something response means the server has screwed something up.
If Art sees that /shipments is happily returning 200s while /exports suddenly starts returning 500s, we now know that the entire application isn’t down at all; something about exporting is broken.

Railway's HTTP Logs tab: a table of requests with method, path, status and response time, mostly 200s and 302s, ending in a POST that returned 502. It is expanded to show the details, including 'failed to forward request to upstream: connection closed unexpectedly'.
Unfortunately for Art, the noble search for one beautiful error message telling you exactly what happened often comes up short. This is when metrics can become useful. Whereas logs tell us about individual events, metrics let us zoom out and look at the overall health of the system.

If users started complaining at 2:17 and CPU hit 100% at 2:16, we have a lead. If memory consumption has been slowly climbing for six hours and then the app crashes, that looks suspiciously like something is “leaking” memory. If network traffic suddenly went vertical, Art may be having another one of those viral moments we dealt with in Part 5.

The trick here is less about any particular number being “bad” and more about looking for something that changed at the same time the app started misbehaving.

A Railway memory usage chart for a service called Memory Hog, climbing in steps from about 1 GB to over 4 GB in two minutes without ever coming back down.
Railway's Metrics tab for a service called cpu-killer: CPU sits near zero until about 8:14 AM, then jumps to roughly 1 vCPU and stays pinned there, with brief drops to zero.
Once you have a decent idea of what broke, the immediate goal is not necessarily to understand every single thing about why it broke. The immediate goal is to keep those potato chips flowing (err… importing / exporting). So, if the app died immediately after a new deployment, just roll it back to the last working one. If the app is simply drowning in traffic, scale it up and buy yourself some breathing room to figure out the root cause.

There’s an important distinction between mitigating an incident and fixing it: mitigation stops the bleeding and gets the app working again, while fixing it means understanding the underlying cause and making sure the same thing can’t take you down next time. This brings us to the other time that you care about observability:

How to prevent an incident

In 1980, about 29 Americans per million died in fires. By 2024, that number was closer to 12. Firefighters have, presumably, gotten better at fighting fires in the intervening decades, but a much larger share of this reduction is owed to improvements in fire detection and prevention. Building codes, smoke detectors, sprinklers, less building-buildings-out-of-kindling-and-illuminating-them-with-candles thing. Said differently, an ounce of prevention was worth a pound of cure.

The same principle applies to keeping an application running. After every incident, once everything is back online and the caffeine shakes have subsided, you should be asking two questions: how could I have known about this sooner, and how could I have prevented it from happening at all?

The first question gets us to alerting. The second gets us to automated action. This is the big-brain, real-engineer way of operating software: gradually taking all the ways your app has surprised you and putting guardrails around them so they stop being surprises.

Alerting

So far, all of our observability has required Art to go looking for something. Elaine tells him the app is down, Art opens Railway, Art looks at his metrics, Art discovers that his app has spent the last half hour fighting for its damn life at 100% CPU. This is better than having no observability at all, but it still requires Elaine.

What we actually want is for the system to notice that something weird is happening and tell Art about it proactively. We want technology to take Elaine’s job. That’s what an alert is: some condition that says, roughly, “this number has gotten bad enough that a human should probably know about it.”

Railway lets you monitor resources in its Observability dashboard for CPU, memory, disk usage, and network egress. Rather than Art periodically opening Railway to make sure everything looks okay, he can decide what “not okay” looks like ahead of time and set up monitors and alerts for it. Maybe the Vandelay app normally uses 20-40% of its available memory, so Art creates a monitor for when it gets above 80%. Now if memory starts climbing toward the limit at 3:00 in the morning, Art gets a notification (email, Slack, whatever) without having to wait for an eager exporter in a more favorable timezone to discover the problem first.

Railway's Add monitor dialog over a metrics dashboard, set to trigger an alert when CPU is above 10 vCPU, with a note that you'll get an email when the monitor is triggered.
The exact threshold you pick is going to depend on the application, and you do not want to alert on every little spike. CPU hitting 80% for five seconds because somebody requested a particularly elaborate potato-chip report is probably fine as long as two users don’t do it at once, but CPU sitting at 95% while response times get worse for twenty minutes is probably worth investigating. The goal is to find conditions that give you useful warning that something is going wrong without turning Art’s inbox into a stream of messages he mostly ignores.

There are other events where the threshold is even simpler. If a production deployment fails, for example, there is not much value in waiting for it to fail really hard before telling someone. Railway can send project events to any system via webhook, which means deployment failures and other events can ultimately make their way into whatever system your team actually pays attention to, whether that’s Slack, Discord, or something more elaborate.

Railway's New Webhook form: a webhook URL field, a note that payloads are formatted automatically for Discord and Slack, and event types to choose from, including Monitor Triggered and Deployment Crashed, Oom Killed and Failed.

<result># R-observability: how ddflow observes itself, and how it should watch observability in managed projects

Evidence marks: [V] I verified it myself, by probe or by reading a primary page. [K] it comes from the plan or from my own knowledge. [W] it is a secondary web source. Nothing was changed except the one research note, R-observability.

## 1. What we HAVE (ddflow observing itself)

**The event log is the telemetry source [V].**
- **Size and shape:** 132,468 events in 834 per-agent shards, 117 MB, 9,021 subjects, from 2026-09-28 to 2026-11-03. Median is 2 events per subject, p90 is 49, max is 959.
- **Schema:** every event has exactly 8 keys: `agent, data, id, kind, lamport, schema, subject, ts` (read from `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl`). A global ordering comes from the Lamport clock.
- **Mix (66 kinds):** `lease.renewed` is 39k events, 29.8% of events but only 8.5% of bytes. `gate.failed` is 34 MB and `gate.passed` is 27 MB, the largest by bytes. Next come `review.triaged` and `task.updated`, around 6 MB each.
- **Retention:** nothing is deleted. `.ddflow/local/archive` is 454 MB, `.ddflow/runs` 98 MB, `.ddflow/local/reviews` 44 MB, and the two `read-snapshot` files 95 MB each.

**Statistics.** `ddflow metrics` is derived from the log (code in `ddflow/services/metrics/`). Measured today:
- **Cycle time (claim to done):** n=1521, p50 1.3 h, p90 8.5 h, max 168 h.
- **Review rounds per item:** p50 4, p90 9, max 40.
- **Queue wait:** p50 60 min, p90 36 h. The glob-conflict share of it has p90 6.1 h.
- **Rework:** 2% (32 of 1709 completed items were hit by a later bug).
- **Time per gate:** ci p50 8 min / p90 27 min, critic 7 / 22, rubber_duck 7 / 21, unit_tests 10 / 24. Queued time for the ci lock or slot is shown separately.
- **Gate outcome rates:** ci fails 38%, critic 55%, rubber_duck 57%, unit_tests 6%. ci is "unavailable" 11% of the time.
- **Other views:** `metrics` also offers `forecast`, `retro`, `skips`, `lanes`, `stages` and `locks`.
- **Caveat:** a critic or rubber_duck "fail" is a review finding, not an outage. It is a quality signal and needs a different SLI than "ci failed".

**Resource metrics.**
- **Capture:** `ddflow/infra/resources.py` takes kernel rusage per child process via `wait4` (cpu, peak rss, block io), with a delta fallback and `unavailable` rather than 0.
- **Coverage today:** only 44 of 22,231 gate outcome events (0.2%) carry it so far, because PM-resource-capture only just landed. Example: LK-observed-globs ci, `maxrss_kb` 1,495,024, `elapsed_s` 1971.9.
- **Host sampling:** `ddflow/infra/signals.py` samples load, free memory and free disk. `core/flowcontrol.py` is an AIMD controller with hysteresis, a cooldown and "N bad of last W" before it decreases (decision D-adaptive-flow-accepted). This is already better alerting hygiene than the article suggests.
- **Governor:** `config_sections/govern.py` has a ladder with a hysteresis margin of 0.05 and 300 s of stillness before stepping down.

**Health, alerts and cadence.**
- **Health:** `ddflow health` (healthwatch) found 26 findings: 24 CRASHED lanes with unmerged work, and 2 IDLE.
- **Modes and thresholds:** modes are off, propose or apply. Thresholds are knobs: idle, stalled, runaway, crashed.
- **Cadence:** `ddflow cadence` lists DUE passes. It is count-based and calendar-based with no daemon (D-sched-no-daemon).
- **Loops and doctor:** both exist. The MCP banner reports "21 queue loop finding(s)".

**Logs.**
- **Logs of ddflow itself:** there is no application logging. `import logging` / `getLogger` has 0 hits in `ddflow/`.
- **What exists instead:** `.ddflow/local/mcp-workers.log` is a 28 KB, 89-line stderr dump (the first lines are a Python traceback from a worker import failure). Gate output goes to `.ddflow/runs/<item>/` and review transcripts to `.ddflow/local/reviews`, both by digest.
- **Redaction:** `core/redact_errors.py`, `secret_shapes.py` and `sensitivity.py` exist, and `[REDACTED:path]` markers appear in events.

**Traces and correlation: absent [V].**
- **No id fields:** no event carries a run id, trace id, tool-call id, prompt id or lane id as a field. Correlation today is `agent + subject + lamport`.
- **Where a request id appears:** only `session.prompt` carries the harness session, inside its text.

**Cost: absent [V].**
- **Gate and review events:** none carries tokens or dollars. Of events whose text mentions tokens or cost, 1,192 are `session.prompt` text and none is a gate-level field.
- **Review latency:** review records only a whole-round `elapsed_s`.

**Alert consumption: weak [V].**
- **Overdue cadence:** `ddflow status` shows `health_watch` overdue by 632,225 s against a 900 s target (about 7 days). `integration_tests` is 1,485 tasks past a cadence of 5, and `dedupe_sweep` is 625 past a cadence of 4.
- **Alerts with no consumer:** an unrun periodic watchdog is the same failure the article warns about, alerts nobody acts on. I read this as a finding about the design, not a bug in a single check.
- **Crashed lanes:** the same 24 crashed lanes sit in both `health` and the brief on every session.

## 2. What we PLAN (existing ids; do not duplicate)

**P-perf-metrics: 37 tasks, 4 done (decision D-perf-metrics-answers).**
- **Done:** PM-env-fingerprint, PM-cycle-split, PM-resource-capture, PM-perf-decide.
- **Open collection tasks:**
  - PM-store: local ring plus committed rollups and daily aggregates.
  - PM-retention: age and size caps, an allowlist redaction pass.
  - PM-selfcost: the telemetry's own overhead as a budget.
  - PM-sampler: live rss and cgroup sampling.
  - PM-agent-calls: tool-call counts and import of Claude Code OTel/session logs.
  - PM-llm-wait: per-request latency, tokens, retries. It already says "names follow OTel GenAI conventions so an exporter can map them".
  - PM-test-durations.
  - PM-remote.
- **Open analysis tasks:**
  - Detection and budgets: PM-detect (regression detector), PM-budgets (a ratchet), PM-flaky.
  - Quality and complexity: PM-quality-signals, PM-complexity.
  - Reports: PM-report-data, PM-report-text, PM-report-charts, PM-report-surfaces.
  - Proposals and review: PM-review-job, PM-prop-flow, PM-prop-llm, PM-prop-tests, PM-auto-apply, PM-observe-bridge.
- **Path telemetry (WP-):** WP-path-collect, WP-path-telemetry, WP-path-variants, WP-gate-yield, WP-merge-detect-gates, WP-path-effect, WP-merge-propose.

**P-observe: 13 open tasks.**
- **Detection and findings:** `.telemetry` (close the telemetry gaps), `.detectors`, `.findings`, `.conformance`.
- **Loop closing:** `.effect`, `.experiments`, `.retro`, `.moments`, `.proposals`.
- **Research:** `.survey` (it already lists "DORA and flow metrics, SRE postmortems and error budgets"), `.cross-project`.

**P-awareness:**
- **Open:** AW-event-classes, AW-sinks (quiet hours, rate limit, dedupe, at-least-once), AW-schedule, AW-gateway-sink, AW-hook-delivery, AW-roadmap-progress, AW-acceptance.
- **Abandoned:** AW-inbox, AW-since-cursor.

**P-operator-digest:** OD-queue is done. OD-sinks and OD-seen are open.

**P-optimizer:** the OPT-* tasks plus the TA-* add-time hygiene tasks. They consume the signals only through replay (OPT-simulate) and conflict history (OPT-history), not through a common metric API.

**Cost:** B-gap-spend is a usage ledger with "UNAVAILABLE, not zero". It is not started because it waits on B-am-ingest and the quota tasks.

**Managed-project side (all open, none started):**
- **P-lifecycle:**
  - LF-feedback: operational signals create PROPOSED items, deduped, capped, with a circuit breaker.
  - LF-trace-edges: defect → release → deployment → incident edges.
  - LF-health.
- **P-architecture-ops:** AR-env-kind (environment with rollback plan and deployed sha), AR-prr (production-readiness checklist), AR-config-drift, AR-fitness-catalogue.
- **P-devsecops-ops, P-security-gate and others:**
  - DS-deploy-verify: drift probe plus rollback and DR drill records.
  - IA-release: environment, deployment and release records with post-deploy gates (smoke, SLO) and a rollback plan.
  - IA-drift: a scheduled read-only plan that files fix items.
  - TF-flows-ops: perf-baseline "thresholds as SLO", deploy smoke and canary.
  - TM-metrics: escape rate and "DORA-like numbers".
  - SC-probe: stack profile (languages, frameworks, existing tool configs, CI commands).
- **P-change-mgmt:** CHG-rollback-required, CHG-plan-fields.
- **P-autopilot:** AP-observe, AP-kill ("any incident demotes automatically").
- **GR-incident:** the leaked-secret incident procedure.

## 3. GAPS

### A. Observability of ddflow itself

1. **No correlation id.** Events have no run, tool-call, prompt or lane id. A causal chain such as "tool call → gate → review → merge → bug" can only be rebuilt by joining on `subject` and time. Claude Code already emits `session.id`, `prompt.id`, `request_id` and `tool_use_id` [V, primary docs]. The cheapest fix is one optional id on events (`data.corr` or an envelope field) plus a stable vocabulary. It must not be a new tracker (r-derive-dont-store).
2. **No request or tool-call log for the MCP server.** The server has no log. The 89-line `mcp-workers.log` is stderr. PM-agent-calls counts harness hook calls, not ddflow's own command latency. The article's point that a request log answers "where" is the real gap here.
3. **No SLIs or SLOs for the tool.** The numbers exist (gate p90, queue age, cycle p90) but nothing says what is acceptable. PM-budgets is a ratchet, not an SLO. The right SLIs are:
   - command latency, such as brief and claim p95;
   - gate time and merge lead time (DORA lead time already exists as cycle time);
   - queue age;
   - a stuck-lane count;
   - "unavailable" rate per gate (ci 11%);
   - the CI false-red rate;
   - log growth (events per item).
4. **Alerting with dedupe and escalation.** healthwatch has thresholds and a mode, and flowcontrol has hysteresis, but there is no common alert state: no dedupe key, repeat suppression, ack, or severity-to-channel map. AW-event-classes and AW-sinks cover this in the abstract. The measured symptom is the 7-day-overdue `health_watch` and 24 crashed lanes re-announced in every brief.
5. **Cost and tokens.** There is no per-gate or per-reviewer cost, only B-gap-spend and PM-llm-wait, both blocked on prerequisites. LLM-reviewer cost is the largest recurring spend (about 11,800 critic and rubber_duck outcomes). Without it, "drop a reviewer" proposals cannot be weighed against yield. WP-gate-yield gives yield but not price.
6. **Exporter.** Nothing maps ddflow signals to OTLP or Prometheus. PM-llm-wait mentions the GenAI names. The honest read is that this is a ddflow-to-others bridge, not something to run as a service inside ddflow.
7. **Post-incident loop for ddflow itself.** Bugs, lessons and regression tests exist and are strong. What is missing is a blameless "incident" view of lane crashes and red main: timeline, detection time, time to recover, and whether a lesson was filed. The data is already in the log (CRASHED, `ci.result`, `bug.found` and `bug.fixed` timestamps).
8. **Privacy.** The allowlist rule is planned (PM-retention), but today's `gate.failed` evidence (34 MB) and `session.prompt` text (5 MB, operator words) are free text. Rule r-secrets still holds, and redaction is by shape, not by schema.
9. **Own overhead.** The committed log grows with perf rollups; PM-selfcost plans a ratchet, but the 30% `lease.renewed` share shows overhead is already large today. I did not verify whether `lease.renewed` is required for liveness.

### B. Observing observability in managed projects

Nothing is planned for any of the following. I searched for logging standards, SLO, runbook, incident, error tracking, OpenTelemetry and post-deploy watch. Hits are only IA-release (SLO as a post-deploy gate), TF-flows-ops, the generic "RUNBOOK doctype" (B-dt-library) and GR-incident.

1. **Detection:** SC-probe records the stack, but not observability facts. It does not look for logging libraries, an OTel SDK or collector config, `/health` endpoints, Sentry/Datadog configs, Prometheus rules, Grafana dashboards, or alert files. All of that is a deterministic file scan, so it is cheap.
2. **Definition of done:** there is no per-feature checklist (logs with ids, metrics, health, redaction, alert/runbook link) and no template.
3. **Gate or periodic review:** no check of whether a diff adds an endpoint, job or external call without any logging, metric or error handling. This would be an advisory gate, with LLM judgement only on top of deterministic signals.
4. **Telemetry consumption:** LF-feedback creates PROPOSED items from "operational signals", but the source adapters are not defined. There is no read-only connector pattern for CI logs, prod logs or metrics. This is where the consent and untrusted-data rules bite hardest (r-consent-outward, r-secrets, r-adapters).
5. **Release and rollback watch:** IA-release has post-deploy gates and DS-deploy-verify has rollback records. A watch window after deploy (compare SLIs before and after, trigger propose-rollback) is not specified. ddflow "records and checks, never deploys" (AR-prr), so the rollback action must stay person-only or a proposal.
6. **Incident record:** LF-trace-edges adds `incident` as an edge endpoint but there is no incident record, no timeline, no link to bug → regression test → lesson.
7. **SLO as a record kind:** only mentioned as thresholds in TF-flows-ops, with no definition, budget or burn state.
8. **Per-project consent and config:** which sources, which credentials, who may read prod data. No schema yet.

## 4. Best practice and tools

- **Golden signals and paging [V, SRE book].** Latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Page on symptoms, not causes. A page must be urgent, actionable, and not automatable. Email alerts become noise; use a dashboard for sub-critical signals.
- **SLO alerting [V, SRE workbook].** The recommended pattern is multiwindow multi-burn-rate: page at 14.4× burn over 1 h and 5 min, page at 6× over 6 h and 30 min, ticket at 1× over 3 days and 6 h. An alert needs both windows over threshold. A simple `for:` duration is rated poor on recall and detection time. For low-traffic systems (ddflow is one: tens of events per hour per lane) the workbook says to aggregate or lower the SLO. So burn-rate math is only worth it for queue-age or CI-red SLIs, not for gate yield.
- **DORA [W].** 2025 added rework rate as a fifth metric: throughput (lead time, deployment frequency, failed-deployment recovery time) and instability (change failure rate, rework rate). The grouping and the year it appeared differ between sources. ddflow already has 2% rework, cycle time, and "bug found after merge". The "deployment" half is meaningless without a deploy record (IA-release).
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI [W, partial].** Secondary sources (Greptime May 2026, Dash0, OpenObserve) say the GenAI conventions are in Development status, i.e. unstable. They are now a separate repo, `open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai`, which the official page confirms ("moved"). I could not retrieve a primary status line, `invoke_agent` / `execute_tool` definitions, or the `gen_ai.client.operation.duration` stability. Two things follow. Don't couple ddflow's schema to these names; map them in an exporter. Check the repo directly before building the mapping.
- **Claude Code telemetry [V, primary].**
  - Metrics: `claude_code.cost.usage`, `token.usage`, `active_time.total`, `session.count`.
  - Events (via the logs signal): `api_request`, `api_error`, `tool_result`, `tool_decision`.
  - Traces: beta and off by default.
  - Exporters: `otlp`, `console`, `prometheus`. There is no file exporter, so PM-agent-calls' "OTel file export" importer must use the session JSONL or an OTLP receiver.
  - Privacy: prompt and tool content are redacted by default (`OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS`, `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS` and others off). `prompt.id` stays off metrics to avoid cardinality.
  - Caveat: cost figures are described as approximations [W]. D-perf-metrics-answers item 6 therefore holds, with the label "approximate" required.
- **LLM and agent observability tools [W only].**
  - Langfuse: open source, self-hosting needs Postgres, ClickHouse and Redis.
  - Arize Phoenix: OTLP-native; its license is reported both as Elastic License 2.0 and as free self-host, so check.
  - Helicone: a proxy gateway; reportedly bought by Mintlify.
  - OpenInference: Arize's conventions on top of OTel.
  - Fit for ddflow: all are heavy services. Under r-external-frontends, ddflow should export OTLP and files and leave the UI to those tools. It should never ship a GUI or require one.
- **Agent incident pattern [W].** In April 2026 an agent wiped a startup's production database and same-volume backups on Railway with one API call under an over-scoped token (PocketOS; I read only secondary write-ups, not the founder's primary thread). The lessons match ddflow's design: scope credentials, require person confirmation for destructive acts, isolate backups, and let the system block, not merely instruct. It is also a reminder that "mitigate by rollback" is not safe when data is involved.

## 5. Railway article, assessed

I read Railway's own guide (`railway.com/guides/debug-production-incident.md`), which is the closer primary source for the article. The article text you gave me is shorter and misses most of the guide's caveats.

**Applies to ddflow:**
- **Logs vs metrics together.** True, and ddflow's log is both: events are the logs, and `metrics` is the aggregate view.
- **Recent changes first.** In ddflow terms: what merged, which config changed, which upgrade applied (`upgrade.applied` has 863 events). This is the fastest diagnosis for a red main, and `ci.result` plus `worktree.merged` already allow it. It belongs in a "main is red" runbook.
- **Mitigate before root cause.** ddflow practices this for lanes (park, break the lease, recover) but not for red main (the D-bugs-fix-now default starts the fix immediately). A "revert first" path would be CHG-class work (P-change-mgmt).
- **Sustained condition rather than a spike, and avoiding noise.** This is already built (flowcontrol N-of-W, cooldowns, hysteresis). The article's version is simpler than ddflow's.
- **Webhooks to chat.** This is AW-sinks and AW-gateway-sink.

**Irrelevant to ddflow:**
- CPU, memory, disk and egress thresholds on a hosted service.
- HTTP status logs and the health check endpoint.
- Platform dashboards, plan tiers (Pro-only monitors), the 500 lines/s log drop.
- Restart policy and image rollback.
- DNS logs.
All of these matter for B only as things to detect in a project.

**Oversimplified or doubtful:**
- **"Rollback first."** The guide itself says nothing about data, schema or migrations. A rollback that restores an image does not undo writes or a migration. Mitigation here also has to cover feature flags, scaling, and whether the previous version can read the data now in the database.
- **Resource thresholds as the main alert.** The SRE book says to page on symptoms (errors, latency), with CPU and memory as causes. The guide's own limits section says container metrics lack per-endpoint latency, so these thresholds miss user-facing failure.
- **"Logs vs metrics" leaves out traces and events.** The guide's own limits section says there is no tracing backend. Neither the article nor the guide covers profiles. For LLM agents, traces and cost are the main signals.
- **Static thresholds with "sustained" rules.** That is the `for:` pattern, which the SRE workbook rates poor on recall and detection time. Burn-rate alerts are better where there is steady traffic.
- **Webhook alerts into Slack/Discord.** Good for awareness, but the SRE book says a page must need human judgement. Posting every deploy failure into chat makes noise.
- **"Automated action."** The text was cut. In the guide this means webhooks, health-gated deploys and a restart policy of up to 10 restarts. For ddflow the equivalent (auto-park or auto-apply) already exists with caps (r-bounded-everything). The article gives no guidance on safeguards for an agent that acts on its own; the PocketOS incident shows why that needs permission scoping.
- **Vibe-coder framing.** It assumes a human reading a dashboard during an incident. That is a different operating model from agents consuming an event log.

## 6. Proposals

No new phase. Every item fits an existing phase. Dependencies below are ones I confirmed exist as task ids; I did not check the others' states beyond "open".

## 7. Proposed rules

1. **Telemetry carries ids, never content.** Every telemetry record carries ids, durations, counts, sizes and hashes; prompt text, command arguments, outputs and paths are excluded by allowlist (builds on r-secrets and PM-retention).
2. **Unavailable is never zero.** Already a ddflow convention; make it a rule for telemetry, with the label "approximate" for anything imported.
3. **An alert needs an owner and a next call.** Every alert class names the exact command that handles it and one dedupe key, and an alert class with no consumer is flagged by `doctor` (addresses the 7-day-overdue `health_watch`).
4. **Imported project telemetry is untrusted data and read-only.** It needs a recorded consent per source, and a source can never trigger an outward action or a deploy.

## 8. Operator questions (recommended defaults)

1. Should ddflow stay a producer of OTLP/files only and never run a collector or a UI? Default: yes, producer only (r-external-frontends).
2. Add a correlation id to events despite the log growth? Default: yes, one short optional id, bounded.
3. May the periodic `health_watch` and the DUE cadences run unattended through a user-installed cron/systemd timer (AW-schedule)? Default: yes, suggested at onboarding, never installed unasked.
4. Is an advisory observability gate acceptable in managed projects, warn-only? Default: yes, off until the stack probe finds the project has any observability.
5. Which telemetry sources may a managed project connect first? Default: CI logs only. Production logs and metrics need a separate consent and read-only credentials.
6. Is "revert first" acceptable for a red main, with a person confirming? Default: propose only, since D-bugs-fix-now is in force.
7. Should the low-traffic SLIs use burn-rate alerts or plain thresholds with N-of-W? Default: N-of-W (already in the code), burn rate only for queue age and CI red.

<result>**Research note filed: `R-scalability`.** Everything below was measured on the real log (132,5xx events, 117 MB, 834 shards) unless marked otherwise. Load average ran 13–66 on 192 cores. Each timing was repeated 2–3 times and I report the min or the range. The scratch scripts are in the session scratchpad.

## 1. Measured profile

**Where one cold load goes** (no profiler, `_load_fresh`):

| Phase | Time |
|---|---|
| import of `ddflow.surfaces.cli` | 0.85 s |
| `read_all` cold | 3.4 s |
| `read_all` warm | 0.5–0.8 s |
| `fold` | 0.9 s |
| `mark`, config, `shardmeta` observe, ticks | under 0.1 s |

Parsing JSON into `Event` objects is 13.7 µs per event (1.8 s). Fold is about 5 µs per event.

**Wall time of the slow commands** (OMP threads capped to 1 for the profiled runs):

| Command | Wall | Where the time goes |
|---|---|---|
| `--version` | 0.99 s wall, **8.2 s user CPU** | `ddflow.services.embed` is imported eagerly by `api.reporting.health`. It pulls numpy, joblib and tokenizers, and OpenBLAS spins about 8 threads. With `OMP_NUM_THREADS=1` user CPU is 0.86 s. |
| `next` | 6–11 s | 2 loads (2 folds), plus a restamp (4 s under cProfile). Planning's glob-conflict check does 76,800 `overlap` calls. |
| `show` | 6–18 s, bimodal | Same loads. With the auto-stamp knob off, cProfile time drops from 22.8 s to 8.0 s. |
| `board` | 9–18 s | 4 loads, restamp, 8 s asleep on the append lock (399 × 20 ms polls), 1.8 MB of output, 32k `_redact` calls (4.4 s under cProfile). |
| `recall` | 15.5 s | The FTS query takes 0.08 s. The other 8 s is the index rebuild: a reconcile plus a full `read_all` and fold. |
| `status` | 22.5 s | 3 folds, and 622 git subprocesses (9.8 s under cProfile) from the recovery scan and `commit_tree_entries`, once per expired lease. |
| `brief` | 40–43 s | 5 folds, 10 `read_all` calls, an index rebuild of 8.4 s, `_sweep_finished` (96 git branch drops, 17 s) and the recovery scan (10 s). |
| `doctor` | about 870 s | py-spy over 150 s put 76% of samples in `verified_level` → `harness.verify` → `find_all`. That rescans 1,264 transcripts (1.3 GB), and a Kilo SQLite table with `json_extract`, once per consumed ask (228 asks). |

**Five findings that are plainly bugs or waste:**

1. **Read verbs restamp whenever any agent writes.** `keep_stamped` compares the global `log.mark()`, so any concurrent writer triggers `waves.restamp`. That runs another load, a fold, the lock and `batch.apply`. It explains the 6 s versus 17 s bimodal pattern for `show`, `list` and `board`.
2. **One command loads the log 2–5 times.** `load_scope` only deduplicates inside the MCP server, not the CLI.
3. **The on-disk read snapshot is slower than not having it.**
   - At 132k events a cold load takes 3.6 s with the snapshot and 2.8 s without.
   - At 1M synthetic events it takes 27 s versus 15 s.
   - It costs 95 MB per fingerprint. Two files sit there now.
4. **The in-process cache is already over its ceiling.** `max_cached_events` is 100,000 against 132,555 events.
5. **The index file name is the hash of the `ddflow/core/**` source.** There are 46 `index.db-*` files totalling 5.0 GB. Each core edit or upgrade means a cold rebuild and another 130 MB file kept for 7 days. A related risk: `decide_then_append` re-runs the read and fold inside the global append lock whenever the mark moved. I inferred this from the code and the board's lock waits; I did not measure lock hold time.

**Complexity per command, with N = events:**

- **O(N), floor about 4.4 s at 132k, times 2–5 loads:** `next`, `show`, `list`, `board`, `status`, `brief`, `recall`, `gate status`, and every write verb's decide step.
- **O(item), possible after a checkpoint:** `show`, `gate status`, `claim`, `heartbeat`.
- **O(expired leases or worktrees) in git subprocesses:** `status`, `brief`, `recover`.
- **O(open tasks²):** `next` and plan.
- **O(asks × transcript bytes):** `doctor`.
- **O(output):** `board`.

**Growth.**

Synthetic log from `services/logfixture.generate`. Its events are smaller than real ones (about 385 B versus 880 B), so real numbers are roughly twice these.

| Events | Cold load | RSS |
|---|---|---|
| 32k (real prefix) | 0.8 s | 185 MB |
| 66k (real prefix) | 1.5–2.1 s | 285 MB |
| 132k | 2.8 s | 555 MB |
| 250k | 3.3 s | 555 MB |
| 500k | 7–8 s | 1.1 GB |
| 1M | 15–30 s | 2.2 GB |

Linear extrapolation gives about 150–300 s and about 20 GB at 10M. That is infeasible.

At 1M a command does 2–5 of those loads, so `next` would take 30–150 s. The real 132k RSS is already 580–700 MB per CLI call, about 4.4 KB per event.

The log grew 2.3k–7.5k events a day over the last 14 days (about 3.3k a day on average). 1M events arrives in roughly 125–260 days. 10M is years away on this trajectory, but a monorepo or a multi-org shared log would reach it sooner.

**Event mix.**

- `lease.renewed` is 29.8% of events but only 8.5% of bytes.
- `gate.passed` and `gate.failed` are 53% of bytes (62 MB), with evidence still largely inline.
- `gate.started`, `gate.out_of_order` and `ddflow.seen` add another 10–12% of events.

**Git.**

- Event commits are about 110 a day, and a git status on the events path takes 16 ms.
- The commit itself is cheap. The git cost is the per-lease and per-worktree subprocess fan-out above.
- `.git` is 240 MB.

## 2. Inventory of persistent stores and caches

| Store | Role | Key and invalidation | Cold / warm | On upgrade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl` (834 shards) | Truth | Append-only, per-agent shard, git-tracked | n/a | Never rewritten; upcasters handle old events |
| `.ddflow/blobs` | Out-of-line gate evidence | Content-addressed | Lazy | Additive |
| `local/read-snapshot-<fp>.bin` (95 MB each) | Marshal of parsed event tuples plus merge order | Version and parser stamp; per-shard prefix sha256; GC by `snapshot_stale_days` | Slower than JSON parsing (finding 3) | New file per version, cold read |
| In-process `_PARSE_CACHE` / `_MERGED`, MCP resident State | Parse and order cache | Shard prefix digest; 100k-event ceiling | Warm read is 0.5–0.8 s | Lost on process exit |
| `index.db-<code-fp>` (+wal/shm/lock; 46 files, 5.0 GB) | SQLite FTS5 projection | Hash of core source; per-shard prefix hashes let the reconcile run, but it still needs a full fold; 7-day GC | Rebuild 8 s | Full rebuild, old one kept 7 days |
| `local/shardmeta`, `local/shard-marks` | High-water marks for loss detection | Updated by `observe` on every load | Cheap | Additive |
| `local/archive` (454 MB), `reviews` (44 MB), `jobs`, `waits`, `baseline`, `ci-failing` | Auxiliary local state | Per feature | n/a | n/a |
| `.ddflow/worktrees` | Agent worktrees | Leases | 7.0 GB, with 39 leftovers and 19 holding work | n/a |

There is no State-level checkpoint. State pickles to 85 MB (`items` is 74 MB) and loads in 0.47 s against 0.9 s for fold. That alone is not enough, because it grows with N.

## 3. Options, with evidence and upgrade safety

Speedups are against 132k cold, about 4.4 s per load.

| Option | Estimate | Effort | Risk | Rollback and soft upgrade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Fix restamp trigger** (own appends only; read verbs never stamp) | `show`, `list` and `board` lose 3–16 s; no more write-on-read | S | Low | Pure code. Behaviour change: waves are stamped only after your own writes. |
| **B. One load per command** | Divides the 2–5× multiplier by 2–5 | S | Low | Pure code |
| **C. Lazy `embed` import plus OpenBLAS thread cap** | 7 s CPU per invocation, about 130 ms wall | XS | Low | Pure code |
| **D. State checkpoint ladder plus tail fold** (upgrade of `UX-incremental-fold`) | About 6× at 132k: load 0.5 s plus `mark` 0.06 s plus tail | L | Medium | See below |
| **E. Hot/cold State** (open items, leases and schedule inputs in memory; finished items' histories and evidence per item from SQLite or a sidecar) | Bounds State size; makes O(item) verbs real; needed beyond about 300k events | L | Medium | Same safety as D; the log is untouched |
| **F. Index reconcile from the checkpointed State**, with the key moved from source hash to explicit `SCHEMA`/`FOLD_REV` | `recall` and `brief` lose the 8 s rebuild; dev edits stop creating 130 MB files | M | Medium | Cap the number of index files, keep the 7-day GC; delete to roll back |
| **G. Lease sidecar** (existing `UX-lease-sidecar`) | −30% of events and future growth; fold work −30% | M | Medium | Old renewals stay in the log and the handler stays; documented loss of cross-clone liveness visibility |
| **H. Faster parse**: lazy `data` (keep raw JSON until a handler needs it) or optional `orjson` extra | Parse is 1.8 s of 2.8 s cold. `orjson` 2–4× is a published figure, not measured here. | S–M | Low | Optional extra with stdlib fallback, byte-identical output |
| **I. Segments / sealed shards** | Cold shards never opened; verify and replay stay full | L | High | Sealing manifest only; **no file moves**, since an older ddflow would then silently miss events |
| **J. Daemon** | Only helps beyond D; `D-sched-no-daemon` stands | M | Medium | Defer until D is measured |
| **K. Output caps** (existing `UX-output-caps`) | `board` 1.8 MB to bounded; render and redaction cost drops | S | Low | Pure code with `--full` |
| **L. Doctor one pass**: index transcripts once per run; memoise by (ask, file, mtime, size) | About 870 s to about 60 s | S–M | Low | Pure code |
| **M. Git batching** (one `for-each-ref`, one `worktree list`, per-HEAD cache); `sweep_finished` out of `brief` | `status` and `brief` lose 10–17 s | M | Low | Pure code |
| **N. Evidence inline threshold** (knob exists) | About half the log bytes for new events only | S | Low | Additive; old events untouched |

**How D stays upgrade-safe.**

- The checkpoint is derived, local and gitignored, like the snapshot. It stores the State before `localize` and `overlay`, the per-shard (size, prefix digest) marks, and the adopted-event set.
- A tail event that sorts before the checkpoint's high key, or a newly adopted event, makes the reader fall back to an older rung and then to a full fold. In the worst case it costs what it costs today.
- The key is an explicit `FOLD_REV`, `SCHEMA` and `FORMAT_LEVEL`, with a test that checkpoint plus tail equals a full fold over a fixture corpus. A source hash would make every dev edit invalidate it, as it does for the index today.
- An older ddflow ignores an unknown-format file and folds fully. Deleting the file, or `DDFLOW_CHECKPOINT=0`, is the rollback. Nothing is written below about 20k events, so small projects change nothing.
- `ddflow upgrade --apply` should pre-warm the checkpoint so the first command after an upgrade is not cold.

**On DuckDB and `D-no-duckdb`.**

- It was already superseded by `D-perf-index`, which keeps "SQLite FTS5 only".
- It revisits an optional analytics extra only past 500k events after checkpoints.
- It sets a compiled-core trigger at fold plus read over 3 s idle, RSS over 1 GB, or over 1M events.
- The evidence says the cost is the Python fold and event materialisation, not query speed. The FTS query is 0.08 s.
- **I do not propose superseding it.** Do D–F first. At 1M events without checkpoints the compiled-core triggers are crossed, so re-measure at the exit gate.

Approvals, rules, decisions and research (4.3k tasks, 1.5k research notes, 352 decisions) are cheap once the fold stops being repeated. FTS5 already exists. The approvals cost is the transcript scan in L.

## 4. Proposal: extend `P-perf`, adding `PS-*` tasks

**Phase home.** `D-scope-focus-2026-11` (5) freezes new phases until open tasks drop below 1,500; roughly 4,100 are open. `P-perf` is open at 0/5, with `B-perf-bench`, `B-perf-lazy-cli`, `B-perf-hook-fast-path`, `B-perf-mcp-start` and `B-perf-memory-footprint` open. Putting this work under `P-perf` avoids the freeze. A separate `P-scale` would need a named user, a falsifier and a kill date.

**Existing tasks to adopt, not duplicate:**
- `UX-latency-profile` can close on this note.
- `UX-incremental-fold`, `UX-lease-sidecar` and `UX-output-caps`
- `snap-log-ceiling` (running)
- `LK-hook-snapshot` (running)
- `FOC-log-ceiling`, `FOC-doctor-slow`, `UX-doctor-budget`
- `B-perf-bench`, `B-perf-lazy-cli`
- `PM-selfcost`, `UX-local-telemetry`

**Duplicates to merge:** `AU-startup`, `B-perf-lazy-cli` and `EX-startup-budget`.

**New tasks.** Sizes: S under 1 day, M 1–3 days, L 1–2 weeks.

| Id | Gist | Needs | Size / risk | Falsifier | Wave |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PS-restamp-own | `keep_stamped` counts only its own appended events; read verbs never restamp | none | S / low | A second process appending in a loop; `show` still calls `batch.apply` | 0 |
| PS-single-load | One `_load_fresh` per CLI command (extend `load_scope`) | none | S / low | A test counting fold calls shows more than 1 per read verb | 0 |
| PS-lazy-embed | Lazy `model2vec` / `embed`; cap BLAS threads at startup | none | XS / low | `--version` user CPU over 1.2 s, or numpy in `sys.modules` | 0 |
| PS-snapshot-calibrate | Default the marshal snapshot off, or write it only when measured faster, until D lands | none | XS / low | Cold load with it on is slower than off | 0 |
| PS-index-cap | Keep at most K index files; fold-rev key instead of source hash (stage 1: cap and GC only) | none | S / low | After 20 core edits there are more than K files | 0 |
| PS-doctor-onepass | One transcript index per doctor run; memoise verification | `FOC-doctor-slow` | S–M / low | Doctor over 60 s idle, or output differs | 0 |
| PS-git-batch | Batched git queries; `sweep_finished` throttled out of `brief` | none | M / low | More than 30 git subprocesses for `status` with 126 stale leases | 0 |
| PS-bench-fixture | Real-mix profile in `logfixture` (research, decisions, `task.updated`); 100k and nightly 1M tiers | `B-perf-bench`, `FOC-log-ceiling` | M / low | Fixture kind mix differs from the real log by over 5 points | 0 |
| PS-state-checkpoint | Checkpoint ladder plus tail fold, with the `FOLD_REV` and equivalence test | `PS-single-load`, `PS-bench-fixture`, `snap-log-ceiling` | L / medium | `show` over 1.5 s idle, or State not byte-identical to a full fold | 1 |
| PS-hot-cold-state | Cold items loaded per id from SQLite or a sidecar | `PS-state-checkpoint` | L / medium | RSS over 500 MB at 1M, or `show` not O(item) | 1 |
| PS-lock-light | The decide step under the lock costs a mark compare plus a tail | `PS-state-checkpoint` | M / medium | Append-lock hold p95 over 100 ms with 20 writers | 1 |
| PS-index-tail | Index reconcile from checkpoint plus tail | `PS-state-checkpoint` | M / medium | `recall` over 2 s after one append | 1 |
| PS-parse-fast | Lazy `data` / optional `orjson` extra | `PS-bench-fixture` | S–M / low | Cold parse under 1.5× faster, or output not byte-identical | 2 |
| PS-evidence-inline | Lower the evidence inline threshold (knob only) | none | S / low | New-event bytes not at least 30% lower | 2 |
| PS-seal | Sealed-shard manifest, no moves | `PS-state-checkpoint`, trigger | L / high | Gate: only if post-D p95 at 1M still breaks budget | 3 |
| PS-core-eval | Re-measure against the `D-perf-index` thresholds (PyO3 or optional analytics extra) | D–F done | M / medium | Budgets met, so nothing built | 3 |

`UX-lease-sidecar` and `UX-output-caps` run in wave 2.

**Performance budget, p95 at 1M events, idle machine.** Today's numbers are at 132k.

| Command | Today | Target at 1M |
|---|---|---|
| `--version` | 1.0 s wall, 8.2 s CPU | 0.3 s |
| hooks | n/a | 0.3 s p50 (per `D-perf-index`) |
| `show`, `list`, `gate status`, `next` | 6–18 s | 2 s |
| `status`, `brief` | 22, 40 s | 3 s |
| `board` | 9–18 s | 3 s, output-capped |
| `recall` / `search` | 15.5 s | 2 s |
| write verbs (`claim`, `heartbeat`, `complete`) | O(N) inside the lock | 2 s; lock hold under 100 ms |
| `merge` | git-bound | 5 s |
| `doctor` (quick / `--full`) | about 870 s | 10 s / 5 min, time-bounded |
| `rebuild` index, `verify`, `replay` | n/a | 5 / 10 / 10 min (linear is acceptable) |
| RSS (read verbs) | 580–700 MB | 500 MB |
| Derived data on disk | about 5.2 GB (index.db files plus snapshots) | at most 3× log size |

The existing `D-perf-index` budgets of 2 s for `status`, `next` and `brief` are already breached by 5–20×.

**Regression ratchet design.**

1. **Fixture.** The generator `services/logfixture.generate` already exists (1M events in 191 s). Add the real-mix profile. Cache fixtures by (seed, size, generator version) under `.ddflow/local/bench`.
2. **Hard-gated deterministic counters:** folds per command, events parsed, git subprocesses, bytes read, modules imported, events appended by read verbs (must be 0), append-lock hold.
3. **Timing.** Use user CPU normalised by a calibration loop, min of 3 runs, with a ±25% noise band. Wall time is informational, because this machine runs at load 60.
4. **Slope test.** Run at N and 4N and assert the ratio is under 2 for O(item) verbs. This holds on any machine speed.
5. **Baseline.** Shrink-only, stored in `tests/perf/baseline.json` and refreshed by `pins regenerate`. The budgets live in `[perf]` knobs.
6. **CI.** 100k tier inside the unit gate (under 60 s); 1M tier as a nightly cadence job. Start as `warn` for 2 weeks, then `block`.

**Proposed rules:**
- `r-perf-budget`: every top-level verb has a budget knob and a test, and a slower verb fails CI.
- `r-read-verbs-read-only`: read verbs append zero events.
- `r-derived-cache-bounded`: every derived store has a fingerprint, a size cap, a GC policy and an env kill switch.
- `r-no-eager-heavy-import`: optional-extra modules are imported only at use.
- `r-single-load`: at most one fold per command.

## 5. Operator questions, with recommended defaults

1. **Home for the work:** extend `P-perf` (default, avoids the intake freeze) or open `P-scale` under the exception rule.
2. **Waves stamped only after your own writes:** read verbs stop restamping. Default: yes.
3. **Checkpoint format and scope:** local, gitignored pickle, written above 20k events. Default: yes. Shared or committed checkpoints stay off.
4. **Retire the marshal snapshot** once D lands; read the old format for two releases. Default: yes, and default it off now.
5. **Compiled core or DuckDB:** keep `D-perf-index` thresholds, no rewrite now, re-measure at the exit gate. Default: no supersede.
6. **Optional `orjson` extra** with a stdlib fallback. Default: yes, optional.
7. **Operational events to a local sidecar:** `lease.renewed` first, then `gate.started`, `gate.out_of_order` and `ddflow.seen` after measurement. Default: yes, with the liveness trade-off documented.
8. **Derived-cache caps:** keep at most 3 index files, plus an auto-prune size cap. Cleaning the 7 GB `.ddflow/worktrees` and the 39 leftovers is your call.
9. **Ratchet enforcement:** `warn` for 2 weeks, then `block`; deterministic counters gate hard, wall time does not.

data.summary: R-scalability finding 1: keep_stamped compares the global log.mark(), so any concurrent writer makes a read verb (show, list, board, next) run waves.restamp: another load, a fold, the lock and batch.apply. Evidence: show is bimodal, 6 s idle versus up to 18 s when another agent appended; with DDFLOW_WAVES_AUTO_STAMP off, cProfile time drops from 22.8 s to 8.0 s. It also makes a read verb write to the log. FALSIFIER/REGRESSION TEST: a second process appends in a loop; a read verb must still make zero batch.apply calls and append zero events (fails against the unfixed code). Fix task: PS-restamp-own. Rule r-read-verbs-read-only. Source: R-scalability.
data.title: Read verbs restamp the waves whenever any agent appends

data.summary: R-scalability finding 2: load_scope deduplicates loads only inside the MCP server, not the CLI. Evidence at 132k events (about 4.4 s per cold load): next does 2 loads, board 4, status 3 folds, brief 5 folds and 10 read_all calls. FALSIFIER/REGRESSION TEST: count _load_fresh and fold calls per read verb; more than 1 fails (fails against the unfixed code). Fix task: PS-single-load. Rule r-single-load. Source: R-scalability.

data.summary: R-scalability finding 3: at 132k events a cold load takes 3.6 s with the snapshot and 2.8 s without; at 1M synthetic events 27 s versus 15 s. FALSIFIER/REGRESSION TEST: a calibration test fails when the snapshot-on cold load is slower than snapshot-off on the fixture. Fix task: PS-snapshot-calibrate. Source: R-scalability.
