data.body: DECISION-type task: ends with a decision record D-hot-cold-tiering (ddflow decision add) and a prototype fixture, no production code. Source: D-scale-answers (3)(4), R-scalability option G/E. Problem: lease.renewed is 30 percent of events, gate.started, gate.out_of_order and ddflow.seen add 10 to 12 percent; they are operational noise to the fold yet part of the evidence trail. Requirements from the operator: several agents work in parallel in several clones on one or many machines; NO evidence or log may be lost; everything stays accessible and searchable; the full log stays the reference for replay, export and edit-by-correction (append-only, nothing deleted or rewritten, r-replay-compat). The design must answer: (1) which kinds are hot and which cold and how that is declared as data; (2) the HOT CACHE and HOT SUMMARY derived from the full log, each cold range referenced by (shard, byte range, digest) so a summary can always be re-expanded; (3) how COLD DATA FROM OTHER CLONES IS SHARED through git: mergeable per-agent shards and committed summaries with references, no merge conflicts, no shared mutable file; (4) how a SECONDARY SEARCH reaches cold data (FTS over summaries with a fall-through to the cold range, bounded); (5) what export, replay, verify and edit-by-correction do with tiers (identical output to today); (6) liveness trade-off if lease renewals leave the log (cross-clone lease visibility) and how a lease expiry is still provable; (7) upgrade safety: old ddflow reads new logs, new reads old, migration with dry run and rollback (r-upgrade-safe, r-replay-compat); (8) failure modes: clone that never pushes, crash mid-write, clock skew, two machines. Output: the decision record, a size model from the 132k-event log, and a falsifier test plan. UX-lease-sidecar, PS-hot-cold-state and any move of operational events out of the committed log wait for it. FALSIFIER: a scenario with two clones and a crash in which any event or evidence blob cannot be recovered, found by search, or replayed. SIZE M, RISK high if wrong. CONFORMANCE (r-upgrade-safe, r-replay-compat, r-derive-dont-store, r-derived-cache-bounded, r-bounded-everything, r-everything-configurable, r-no-shell, r-tell-dont-discover, r-unavailable-not-pass, r-docs-with-the-change, D-scale-answers, D-scope-focus-2026-11, R-scalability): the event log is never rewritten or truncated; every cache is derived, local and rebuildable; old logs replay identically; a new knob defaults to the old behaviour; an upgrade note ships with the change; a measurement that could not run is unavailable; a fix carries a regression test that fails against the unfixed code.

data.body: Rule r-perf-budget. BUDGET, p95 at 1M events on an idle machine (today at 132k): --version 0.3 s wall (1.0 s wall, 8.2 s CPU); hooks 0.3 s p50; show/list/gate status/next 2 s (6 to 18 s); status and brief 3 s (22 and 40 s); board 3 s and output-capped (9 to 18 s); recall/search 2 s (15.5 s); write verbs claim/heartbeat/complete 2 s with append-lock hold under 100 ms; merge 5 s (git-bound); doctor quick 10 s, --full 5 min time-bounded (about 870 s); rebuild index 5 min, verify 10 min, replay 10 min (linear is acceptable); RSS of read verbs 500 MB (580 to 700 MB); derived data on disk at most 3 times the log size (about 5.2 GB). The existing D-perf-index 2 s budgets for status/next/brief are breached by 5 to 20 times. RATCHET: (1) fixture from PS-bench-fixture; (2) HARD-GATED deterministic counters: folds per command, events parsed, git subprocesses, bytes read, modules imported, events appended by read verbs (must be 0), append-lock hold; (3) timing is user CPU normalised by a calibration loop, min of 3 runs, plus or minus 25 percent band; wall time is informational only; (4) slope test at N and 4N, ratio under 2 for O(item) verbs; (5) shrink-only baseline tests/perf/baseline.json refreshed by pins regenerate, budgets as [perf] knobs; (6) CI: 100k tier in the unit gate (under 60 s), 1M tier as a nightly cadence job; ENFORCEMENT starts as warn for 2 weeks, then block (r-safe-by-default). Also the import-time table (-X importtime top modules). WHY: R-perf-profile-2026-10-11: every number we have was measured by hand in a scratch directory under load 30-300 on 192 cores; without a ratchet the 0.19 s import (R-perf-100k) became 0.5 s unnoticed and status grew to 5.4 s. NOTHING hardcoded: budgets, thresholds for the native-core triggers of B-perf-decide (fold seconds, RSS, event count) and the commands list are config; doctor prints a NOTE when a stored result exceeds a budget or a trigger threshold. TESTS: budgets parse and are honoured (a fake slow command exceeds, exit 1); load-noise flag; CLI/MCP parity; scratch clone leaves the live store untouched (hash of .ddflow before/after); a failing-first test per knob (dead-knob ratchet). SIZE: medium (~500 lines plus tests). ACCEPTANCE: a table for this repository in a research record, a cadence entry that fails when a budget is exceeded by more than the configured margin, README/ARCHITECTURE documented.

WHAT: `ddflow --version`, `--help` and every hook subcommand currently import the whole CLI: cpu 0.53 s for `import ddflow.surfaces.cli` (-X importtime: ddflow.api 0.56 of 0.62 s total, ddflow.api.knowledge 0.18, ddflow.api.ci 0.18, ddflow.config 0.07, jinja2 0.04, services.export 0.06, upgrade_apply 0.07) against 0.04 s for bare Python, measured under load (about half idle). Make command dispatch lazy: the registry maps a command name to a module path and imports that module only when invoked (argparse parser construction from declared data stays cheap, or the parser for one command is built on demand); keep jinja2/tomlkit lazy until first use; hooks import only infra.log, the redactor and the session service. WHY: R-perf-profile-2026-10-11; it is the floor of every agent action that runs a ddflow process (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, git hooks, every CLI call). D-compat: no behaviour change; the existing hoisting work (R9ce3581787: 36 deferred imports hoisted) pushed the other way - cycles stay broken through the registry, not function-local imports, and the earlier tests that forbid function-local imports must keep passing. INTERFACE TO REUSE: surfaces/registry.py and declared/ tables, the single parser source of CLI+MCP parity (mcp.py must still list all 112 tools from the same table). TESTS: failing-first import-budget test: `python -X importtime -c 'import ddflow.surfaces.cli'` imports no module under ddflow.api/ddflow.services except those the command needs (assert by module set, not by milliseconds, so it is load-proof) plus a measured-budget check through B-perf-bench; full CLI/MCP parity and help-text goldens unchanged. SIZE: medium (~300 lines, touches hot files: expect to wait for B-hot-files). ACCEPTANCE: `ddflow --version` cpu under 4x bare Python startup on the same machine; before/after table in a research record; no golden changed.

Test-suite duration extension 2026-10-12 (R-test-duration-2026-10-12): the suite spawns the CLI through 4,635 run_cli call sites in 378 test files (a real python -m ddflow each, 0.615 s for --version measured), 245 cpu-minutes in all; on the 4-vCPU CI runner that is the 78-minute run. Lowering the cold start is worth a measurable share of suite time: add the suite's cpu-minutes (fix-test-duration-profile report) to this task's before/after table. Removing the calls is fix-test-duration-cut; the two stack.

OPERATOR 2026-10-17 (D-unify-deps-r2): lazy loading is the method of the whole performance phase: besides import time, the goal is the smallest memory footprint and fastest startup; coordinate with B-perf-memory-footprint and B-perf-lazy-deps (dependencies imported at the point of use, including the new required PyYAML).

Related: PS-lazy-embed (bug B4c7b7e8d5b, 8.2 s CPU on --version). MERGE PROPOSAL (note only, operator decides): AU-startup, B-perf-lazy-cli and EX-startup-budget overlap on import time and could be one task.

ddflow --version takes 1.1 s because 829 ddflow modules import first; ddflow.api costs 866 ms of 907 ms; every hook call pays it. Lazy per-verb imports, a fast path for --version and hook calls, and an import-time budget ratchet. ALSO COVERS the UX proposal UX-lazy-imports (next on a small project under 300 ms). Do the UX-latency-profile table first if it exists. SIZE M, RISK medium. FALSIFIER: --version over 0.4 s (target 0.3 s). Evidence: ddflow --json show DX-reviewer-independence-soft, ci failed 2026-11-03T16:54:09Z on tree a3c71f95f.

Write the regression test first and watch it FAIL on the unfixed code; then `ddflow complete fix-B0cdef4bf3a --regression-test <test>` closes the bug with the task (or `ddflow bug fixed B0cdef4bf3a --regression-test <test>` first).

<result>The test is fixed and merged to main, but the item isn't completed. `ddflow_complete` is blocked on reviewer independence, and I've requested approval Q72444a9f1a for the override.

**Root cause.** Neither xdist load nor Python 3.14 is the cause. A child reaped with `wait4` reports an `ru_maxrss` that includes the parent process's own peak memory. The kernel folds the parent's high-water mark into the child at exec. A cheap `true` run from a process that had touched 600 MB reported 629760 KB, against 15360 KB before (3.13 and 3.14 alike). So whenever the pytest worker's peak exceeds the 150 MB test child, `cheap == heavy` and `again.maxrss_kb < heavy.maxrss_kb` fails. The old assertion fails deterministically in a 400 MB parent (437760 vs 437760).

I could not reproduce the failure itself. 48 parallel stress processes on 3.14 passed, and the full `-n 48` run on 3.14 was cut off by `-x` at 17 unrelated failures, none in this test.

**Fix, in `tests/test_resource_capture.py` only (7.7 KB).** The per-command test now compares against the test process's own peak, not absolute sizes:
- The heavy child allocates that peak plus 200 MB.
- The test asserts `heavy ≥ own peak + 150 MB` and `again ≤ own peak + 64 MB`, which a running total would break.
- A new regression test, `test_a_cheap_command_in_a_big_process_does_not_fail_the_per_command_check`, runs the same check inside a 400 MB parent.

The file passes on 3.13 and 3.14, serially and at `-n 48`. Merged as 2007f5e3; main's ci passed.

**Production bug, filed:** Bd36ace0ccb. The same inheritance means gate evidence `maxrss_kb` for cheap commands is really the ddflow process's own peak. The test fix doesn't change that.

**Not completed.** The cross-family review hung with no output for more than 40 minutes and was stopped, so `rubber_duck` and `critic` are recorded `unavailable`. `ci` is partial: 6 baseline-red failures, and `test_resource_capture.py` is not among them. `unit_tests` passed (26 tests), though with a local command that differs from the committed one. `ddflow_complete` also needs `--regression-test` to close the bug with the item, which I passed. After the operator approves Q72444a9f1a, re-run complete with that approval id.

**ddflow defects seen:**
- `ddflow_bug found` doesn't accept `evidence`, although the other bug actions document it.
- `ddflow gate record` takes `--exit-code`, while the MCP tool takes `exit_code`.
- `ddflow review` can hang indefinitely on a small diff without timing out. I did not file this one.</result>

<summary>Agent "Research tiny-fix fast track" finished</summary>
<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>Research note **R-tiny-fix-fast-track** is filed (verdict CONFIRMED, attached to P-batch-gates). The sources I opened for it are on the note. The measurement script and its data are in the session scratchpad, not in the repo.

Three results change what to build.
- **Tiny fixes are a small share of the work.** They are about 11% of completed items and 5% of gate-hours, so a fast track is a latency and attention win, not a throughput win.
- **Skipping reviews is not safe.** Reviewers still confirmed a real MEDIUM-or-higher finding in about 15–20% of tiny fixes.
- **Text cannot predict tiny.** The predictor over title, body and globs is barely better than chance, so the diff has to decide after the fact.

## 1. Measurements on the real log

**Method.** I read 133,458 events from `.ddflow/events` (2026-09-28 to 11-03). I joined 1,510 completed items that have a `worktree.merged` event to `git diff --numstat landed_before..landed_after`, excluding `.ddflow` and `docs/ddflow`. The 631 fixes are tasks that start with `fix-`, carry the `bugfix` tag, or have a `fixes` field. Gate times are wall-clock from `gate.started` to `gate.passed` or `gate.failed`, so they include reviewer queue waiting.

**Size.**

| Group | Median changed lines | Items at ≤10 lines |
|---|---|---|
| All items | 200 | 152 |
| Fixes | 102 | 51 |

- The fix diff includes its regression test, which has a median of 64 lines. So the line limit has to apply to source and config lines only, with tests and generated pins counted separately.
- I counted source (`ddflow/` outside templates) and other non-test, non-doc files. The median fix has 31 source lines; 198 of 631 fixes have 10 or fewer and 121 have zero.
- 106 fixes touch only tests, docs or config.

**Definition that fits the data (tiny-cold).** A fix is tiny-cold when it meets all of these:
- Source plus other lines are at most 10.
- It touches at most 6 files, of which at most 2 are source.
- No path falls in the hot engine set: `core/`, `services/enforce*`, `lease*`, `hooks`, `services/gates`, `api/lifecycle`, `adapters/`, `config.py`.
- Generated pins and `README.md` do not count toward the line limit. They are regenerated, and 25 of the 169 tiny-cold fixes touch them.

That gives 169 items, 11% of the total. A looser limit of 20 lines gives about 140 fixes, and only 56 fixes at 5 lines.

**Cost.**

| Measure | Tiny fix | Other fix |
|---|---|---|
| Median lead time, start to complete | 37 min | 87 min |
| ci gate, median | 475 s | 748 s |
| unit_tests gate, median | 560 s | 756 s |
| rubber_duck gate, median | 272 s | 792 s |
| critic gate, median | 195 s | 677 s |
| Triaged findings per item | 0.9 | 5.4 |

- Tiny-cold items spent 70 of the 1,415 gate-hours (5%) on ci, unit_tests, standards and the two reviews. Mean review wall time per tiny-cold item is about 11 minutes.
- The pipeline is fixed per item and ci and unit_tests dominate, so a bundle shares them.
- Rounds: tiny fixes failed rubber_duck 0.47 times and critic 0.4 times per item, against 1.7 and 1.5 for other fixes. ci failed 0.69 times per item.
- Skips and unavailable outcomes were about the same as for larger items: ci was unavailable on 15% and unit_tests on 13%.

**Safety.**
- A confirmed HIGH-or-MEDIUM review finding appeared in 13 of 94 tiny fixes (14%). The rate is 7 of 37 for tiny-cold items that touch source and 23 of 112 for those that touch only tests, docs or config.
- Other fixes have 54% (293 of 537). Findings rise steadily with size: about 5% at 6–10 lines, 17% at 11–20, 50% at 21–50, and 75% above 100.
- Findings on tiny items are real. For example `fix-B-fixtask-globs-omit-test` got two HIGH findings, so review skipping is not free.
- Rework is unmeasurable from the log. `bug.found.item` is empty, and `item.reworked` fires only 5 times.
- As a weak proxy, a later bug or task text mentions the item id or sha for 23% of tiny fixes (22 of 94) against 37% of other fixes.
- A later fix landed on the same source file within 7 days for 50% of tiny fixes against 67% of others. Hot files dominate that number.
- I found no evidence that tiny fixes cause more rework, and also no strong evidence that they cause less.

**Predictor.** Precision and recall for "will turn out tiny", against a 15% base rate among fixes:

| Predictor | Precision | Recall |
|---|---|---|
| Narrow declared globs (at most 2, no `**`) | 0.17 | 0.38 |
| Keywords (typo, wording, docstring, and similar) | 0.19 | 0.30 |
| Globs or keywords | 0.18 | 0.61 |
| Body at most 600 characters | 0.24 | 0.51 |
| Id contains `Bci` (CI-lint bugs) | 0.48 | 0.12 |
| Bug severity (low / medium / high) | 11% / 14% / 20% | not computed |

- 250 of 631 fixes declare no globs at all.
- The pre-work predictor is therefore a hint only, good enough for ordering. It must never grant the lighter pipeline.
- The post-hoc guard has to decide, on the actual diff, exactly as `services/docsonly.py::pipeline_by_diff` already does for `doc_pipeline`.

**Bundling potential.** The 169 tiny-cold fixes completed on 29 days, 5.8 a day on average and at most 12. Of 535 same-day pairs, only 12 (2%) share a path. So path-disjoint bundles are easy, and a cap of 10 is rarely reached. A time trigger matters more than the count.

## 2. Options

Reference numbers: tiny-cold gate wall is about 25 minutes per item (ci, unit_tests, two reviews). Across 169 items that is 70 gate-hours (about 5% of all gate time), or about 40 hours of shared gates if bundled in fives.

**a) Bundle up to N fixes (default 10) into one task, branch, ci run, review and merge.**
- The bundle shares the full ci and unit_tests once, plus one combined review over the bundle diff, which is under the 150-line `combined_under_lines` limit for ten 10-line fixes.
- Estimated saving: about 40–60% of tiny-cold gate wall (roughly 30–40 of the 70 hours). That is 2–3% of total gate-hours but about half of each fix's lead time. A bundle of 5 pays about 25 minutes instead of 125.
- Keep per-fix attribution: one commit per fix, merged with `--no-ff` or with the per-fix commits preserved, so a single revert or bisect works.
- Each fix keeps its own regression test, with the proof that it fails before the fix run in that fix's own tree. Each bug is closed per fix via `bug fixed --regression-test`.
- Failure modes:
  - A red bundle needs a culprit search. Reuse `services/bisect.ddmin` with at most 8 runs, as in D-BG-5. Tiny fixes make that cheap, and the culprit is dropped while the rest land.
  - Flaky tests: use the repeat guard from D-BG-5.
  - Path overlap: a bundle member that overlaps another is refused. This is rare (2%) but must be enforced, along with a pin-file exclusion.
  - Hot shared files: refuse any member that touches `README.md`, `ddflow/surfaces/**`, `config.py` or the golden pins. Pins are regenerated once per bundle.
  - Lease contention: one lease holds the union of the members' globs, so a bundle of ten holds more files longer. Cap the union and the age (the D-BG-4 default is 45 minutes).
  - A member that grows past the limit when the diff is measured is demoted out of the bundle and takes the full pipeline.
- Extend: this is P-batch-gates in spirit, but P-batch-gates batches existing parallel items at the merge queue. This option bundles at authoring time into one item. The two compose, and the merge-queue batch can later pick up the finished bundles.

**b) Risk-tiered gate lightening for tiny-cold, post-hoc guarded.**
- Lightening means one combined, single-round reviewer pass (the existing `combined_under_lines`, today only for fewer than 150 changed lines), with no second round. Plus the deterministic checks, narrowed unit_tests, and the shared full ci.
- Keep per item: research and rules, the regression test failing before the fix, the lint, build and security hooks, `dedupe`, and `bug_hunt` (D-BG-Q7 keeps those per item).
- Estimated saving per item: about 3–5 minutes of 11 minutes of review wall, plus no second round. That is a smaller win than (a).
- Do not skip the review outright. The measured miss rate of 14–20% is too high, and D-BG-Q4 (operator, 2026-10-22) says a tiny batch never skips the second reviewer. Only a new operator answer could reopen that.
- The invariants cannot be skipped:
  - A regression test that fails first.
  - Unavailable is never passed (r-unavailable-not-pass).
  - A post-hoc guard on the actual diff demotes the item to the full pipeline when lines, files or paths exceed the limits. That demotion is recorded and cannot be argued away.
  - Reviewer independence stays soft (D-reviewer-independence-soft): different family, then different model, never the author's own model.
  - Operator approvals stay.
- The guard follows the `doc_globs` precedent: the diff decides, and a required gate is not excused by what a task says it will touch.

**c) Fast-track lane and optimizer ordering.**
- Cheap predicted candidates carry a tag (the existing `bugfix`, `tier:fast`, or a new `fast-track` tag). The optimizer places them back to back, grouped by glob compatibility.
- Evidence: 5.8 tiny fixes a day with 2% path overlap means grouping them costs almost no conflicts. The cost of a wrong prediction (precision about 0.2) is only a wrong order, because the guard still decides the pipeline.
- Extend `TA-fastlane` and `TA-knobs`. They exist but only count phase-less DX and bugfix tasks against a cap; they do not group or pipeline anything. Extend the OPT work (`OPT-signals`, `OPT-tags`, `OPT-order-v2`) with a `batch-with` or affinity term and `WP-merge-detect-tasks`, which proposes task groups that could share a lane and gate pass.

**d) Auto-merge on green.** Both the PR and the merge-queue paths already exist. Auto-merge when the guard passes and all gates are green is a small addition and carries no new risk beyond (b).

## 3. Practice from elsewhere

- **[V] GitHub merge queue.** It has a minimum and maximum group size (1 to 100) and a timeout after which a smaller group merges, plus a separate build-concurrency setting. A blog quotes defaults of 1, 5 and a 5-minute wait, which I did not verify. That matches the size-and-age trigger in D-BG-4.
- **[V] Zuul.** The dependent pipeline tests each change as the speculative future state of everything ahead of it, and on failure drops the failing change and retests the ones behind it. Only changes within the window get jobs. A 2018 mailing-list proposal describes a bisecting pipeline that splits a failed batch in half; it was a proposal, not a documented feature.
- **[V] Google TAP.** Presubmit is limited to the relevant tests, and postsubmit runs everything close to HEAD. Automated culprit finding covers postsubmit breakages, and a newer approach uses Bayesian noisy binary search instead of plain bisect. A "Speculative Cycles" approach prioritises tests likely to fail newly.
- **[V] Chromium.** TBR (post-commit review) is allowed for documentation and for clean reverts of recent patches, but not for urgency. Mechanical changes have a separate path. A trivial-change exemption therefore exists only for a strict, named class, which matches the docs-only and chore precedents here.
- **[V, secondary] SmartBear/Cisco.** Defect discovery falls above about 200–400 changed lines; the figures come from write-ups of the 2006 study, not the paper. D-BG-6 already uses 400.
- **[V, secondary] DORA.** I found no primary DORA finding that smaller batches lower the change-failure rate. Sources attribute lower failure rates to automation and testing rather than batch size alone.
- **[K] Bors and homu.** They batch ready PRs, test the combined merge, and on failure bisect the batch.
- **[K] Uber SubmitQueue.** It speculates builds and orders by predicted change conflicts; a conflict analyser does the grouping.
- **[K] Google's change-size study.** Google's published change-size study found most changes touch one file and are small, which is why small-CL review is cheap and sometimes lightened. I have not re-checked the numbers.

The common pattern is to batch the test and merge cost, keep review per change or per size unit, and rely on automatic culprit search when a batch goes red. Nobody skips review on predicted triviality alone; exemptions are limited to named, mechanical classes.

## 4. Proposal

No new phase. Everything fits in existing phases and extends rather than duplicates.

**Existing work to extend.** `BG-trigger`, `BG-ci`, `BG-fanout`, `BG-review`, `BG-measure` and `BG-record` already cover the shared ci run, the ddmin culprit search and line-sized review units. `TA-fastlane` and `TA-knobs` cover the fast-lane cap. `OPT-tags` and `OPT-order-v2` cover affinity tags and ordering. `WP-merge-detect-tasks` and `WP-opt-merge-decision` cover grouping. `WP-gate-stages` covers the pipeline shape. Tasks below depend on these, which I checked in the log.

**Proposed tasks.** All sizes are estimates; waves are suggestions.

| Id | Title | Phase | Needs (verified) | Size | Risk | Wave |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FT-measure | `ddflow metrics tiny`: tiny-cold counts, per-gate seconds, confirmed-finding and rework rates, so the knob values can be tuned | P-perf-metrics | none | S | low | 1 |
| FT-guard | Post-hoc diff guard as a pure function (lines, files, paths) with a demotion event | P-gate-flow | none | M | medium: mis-demotion | 1 |
| FT-pipeline | `[gates].fast_pipeline` applied by the guard, via the `pipeline_by_diff` pattern | P-gate-flow | FT-guard, WP-gate-stages | M | medium | 2 |
| FT-bundle | One task, branch and ci run for up to N path-disjoint tiny fixes, with per-fix commits, bug closure and culprit drop | P-batch-gates | BG-fanout, FT-guard | L | medium | 3 |
| FT-lane | Tag `fast-track` plus an optimizer glob-compatibility group term and a batch cadence | P-optimizer | OPT-tags, OPT-order-v2, TA-fastlane | M | low | 3 |
| FT-automerge | Auto-merge a fast-track item or bundle when the guard passes and all gates are green | P-lane-consolidation | FT-pipeline | S | low | 3 |
| FT-replay | Replay the 169 tiny-cold fixes through the bundler and guard to check the falsifier | P-optimizer | FT-bundle, OPT-simulate | M | low | 4 |

- **Falsifier (overall).** The replay shows less than 20% gate wall time saved, or more than one culprit-attributed red bundle in ten, or the guard demotes more than 40% of bundled items.
- **Knobs.**
  - `[fasttrack].mode = off|bundle|lighten` (default off).
  - `max_bundle` (10).
  - `max_src_lines` (10), `max_files` (6), `max_src_files` (2).
  - `hot_globs` (the engine set above).
  - `bundle_max_age_min` (45).
  - `auto_merge` (false).
  - `tighten-only` company floors.
  - Each settable by file, env, CLI, MCP and prompt (r-everything-configurable).
- **Upgrade safety.** Every knob is off by default, and the new events are additive (r-upgrade-safe). With mode `off`, behaviour is today's.
- **Rule.** No new rule. r-bounded-everything, r-evidence-over-assertion, r-unavailable-not-pass and r-small-files already cover it. The one new invariant, a guard that demotes and never promotes, belongs in a decision, not a rule.
- **Interaction.** `chore` already skips gates for a configured file class (rules, decisions, generated views) under standing approval, so tiny code fixes must not enter it.

6. Keep `ddflow chore` unchanged and out of this? Default yes.

## 2. The workflow and its mapping

Each stage is a research or task item (kind `research`, `task` or `doc`) with the named records and gates. Every dynamic step runs only in an environment class that TM-safety allows.

| Stage | Records | Gate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Target and authorization | `target` record (TM-target pin plus artifact hash, license and EULA note, purpose, ownership); `attestation` of authorization with an expiring scope | **authorization** (person-only; nothing in stages 3-4 starts without it) |
| 2 Legal and licensing review | research note with sources, plus an attestation of the clean-room mode chosen (non-clean-room, or a spec team and an implementation team) | **legal-review** (person-only; ddflow never decides legality) |
| 3 Artifact acquisition | artifacts stored as hash pointers outside git (like RS-sci-data); a provenance entry (source, date, hash, how obtained) | **provenance**; **no-third-party-artifact-committed** |
| 4 Static analysis | observations as research notes: claim, evidence blob, coverage, an explicit unknown list, confidence; MCP tool output is capped and fenced | provenance (every claim cites an artifact hash and offset) |
| 5 Dynamic observation | `observation` records: trace or capture blob, environment fingerprint, redaction status | **sandbox-isolation** (no network or secrets, resource limits, SEC-sandbox); **scrub** (secrets and PII) |
| 6 Behaviour specification | the requirement kind with class `compat`, linked to observations through the trace engine | provenance; clean-room (spec authors are not implementers) |
| 7 Oracle building | `oracle` fixtures (recorded I/O corpus, built on the evalfixture pattern); hash-pinned; the corpus is sanitised before any later stage may see it | scrub; fixture-integrity check |
| 8 Clean-room handoff | a handoff record carrying only spec ids and oracle ids; the implementer lease is denied read access to the target and analysis paths (lease globs) | **clean-room separation** |
| 9 Implementation | normal tasks that cite `capability` ids; TDD or QA-f2p-task | standard gates |
| 10 Parity measurement | derived `capability` matrix: capability, status, oracle coverage, pass rate, last run at the SUT pin and implementation sha | **parity gate**: differential pass rate against a threshold; an unrunnable oracle is unavailable, never a pass |
| 11 Regression and drift watch | scheduled job: new target version means rerun the oracle and diff the behaviour (MR-drift-report, MR-schedule-audit, P-drift) | drift warns; proposes items only |
| 12 Findings documentation | an exported report with provenance (RS-sci-export pattern) | provenance |

**Debugging your own project.** Hypothesis-driven debugging fits the research kind and needs no new phase:
1. Reproduce: a failing test or a deterministic probe.
2. Bisect with `ddflow bisect`.
3. Trace.
4. Log each hypothesis as a note with claim, falsifier, probe and probe_output, and mark it REFUTED when disproved.
5. Write a root-cause note (RS-templates).
6. Add a regression test that fails before the fix. A bug is already blocked from closing without one.

**Not building.** Recorded-I/O corpora, characterization tests and approval-style golden-master tests are the oracle idea for legacy migration. The strangler fig is the capability matrix hitting 100 percent module by module. These follow Feathers and Fowler [K].

## 3. Tooling landscape (adapter or companion, never built in-tree)

All adapters follow r-adapters (one port per function), the tool-catalogue rows, the unavailable-not-pass rule, a cap on output size, and redaction before storage. Anything that executes the target runs in a sandbox. Nothing is installed without consent.

- **Disassembler and decompiler MCPs:** Ghidra, IDA and Binary Ninja servers. Treated as read-only, local only, with output capped and fenced as untrusted. Licensing is the operator's own.
- **Agent-layer RE tools:** REA is a **peer** (it is also an MCP server). Integration means ingesting its evidence output as an observation, not embedding it. Be aware its runtime mode is not a sandbox.
- **Debuggers and recorders:** gdb, lldb, rr and WinDbg. Record-and-replay is the best match for a reproducible observation.
- **Tracers:** strace, ltrace, eBPF, Frida and dtrace. These execute or attach to the target, so they need an authorization scope and a sandbox. I do not describe evasion.
- **Protocol analysers:** Wireshark/tshark and mitmproxy, producing capture blobs that must be scrubbed.
- **Emulators and VMs:** QEMU and containers as the isolation substrate for the sandbox-isolation gate.
- **Differential and conformance suites:** protocol conformance suites (as in Samba and Wine), plus differential harnesses built on the oracle fixtures.
- **Comparable practice:**
  - Malware-analysis labs: isolation, case management, and IOC provenance (CAPE, FLARE-VM, MISP/STIX) [K].
  - CTF teams: shared notes and hypothesis logs [K].
  - Clean-room history: Compaq/BIOS and ReactOS/Wine, with the ReactOS split definition verified above.

data.summary: A late review recorded while an item is parked (no lease) replaces the approved gate skip and reopens the gate with untriaged findings (DX-reviewer-independence-soft rubber_duck, 2026-11-04T00:16Z); an approved skip should stand until the code it covered changes

The ci gate is recorded failed, not baseline-red, when a non-test check (ruff lint) fails alongside baseline-red tests, so auto-accept never applies and merge/complete need an override (LK-conflict-probe); the gate should split the lint failure from the baseline-red tests and name which check blocks

The ci gate record lists only about 50 of the 283 failing tests, so a person or agent cannot tell from the record whether every failure is baseline-red; the full failing list should be stored in a blob the record links
unit_tests refuses to start while ci is skipped or failed (rerun ci first), so a gate that could pass on its own cannot run; the dependency of unit_tests on ci should be a warning or a knob

A lease runs out while its item waits in the suite queue or its gates run (lk-probe ran out 2 hours before merge); the gate runner or queue should keep the item's lease renewed while a gate of the item is queued or running
Force-act approval requests (claim.force, complete.force) carry an empty agent reason (push-2, push-3, repair-drv), so the person sees no why; a force request without a reason should be refused

Completion over unmet conditions reports 'independence: no reviewer ran at all' although rubber_duck and critic skips were approved and recorded (DX-reviewer-independence-soft); the message should distinguish skipped-under-approval from never-ran

The regression-test check of ddflow complete runs the named test against the pre-fix tree, which passes for a test-only fix (fix-B0cdef4bf3a), so completion needs a mutation workaround; support a declared mutation or a test-only fix kind
ddflow approvals log has no --limit or --since and is very slow on this log (minutes); an approvals audit needs a bounded query

ddflow decision add requires --decision and treats --body-like text as unrecognized; and ddflow has update but task update is an invalid choice: command naming is inconsistent for agents (decision add --decision, update ID --append-body, task add)

The reviewer entries kimi-k3 and the jemmtec reviewers read their key only from an environment variable while only gemini declares api_key_file, so agents must export keys by hand; kimi-k3 shows gates= empty although it should hold critic and rubber_duck
Gate skip outcomes are displayed as 'skipped after a failed run' even when the skip was approved with exact counts, which hides the approval id and the counts from ddflow show

<result>The full report is written, with URLs for every claim and unverified items marked. It adds one finding you didn't ask for: the threshold is not the biggest cost; red main and hub fallbacks are. That comes from 1,132 timed `ci` records in the event log.

**What the log shows**
- **Artificial queue:** the full suite costs about 20 CPU-hours, and 16 runs a day use only about 7% of this host's 192 logical CPUs. One slot still saturates; 22 Oct logged 31.8 run-hours in a day.
- **Waiting:** since 28 Oct, 150 of 283 runs waited, and those spent about half their time waiting. So "most of their time" holds only for the worst cases.
- **Why runs go full:** 63% of the 238 full runs are hub fallbacks, and 73% of those come from `services.gates`, `config` and `surfaces.mcp`.
- **Red main:** no selected run recorded `gate.passed` in 1-4 Nov (0 of 216). I did not separate red-main failures from real ones.
- **Stale memory:** the "48 s at -n 48" note is about 40x off; the median full run takes 1,868 s.

**Techniques that transfer best** (evidence: A strong, B moderate, T my inference)
1. **Token-weighted admission (A pattern):** tokens equal xdist workers, with cost predicted from per-file CPU history and capacity from cores. File count ranks runs well (Spearman 0.94, n=46) but misprices them about 6x. This should remove most of the 37% wait here and still work on a laptop.
2. **PSI plus memory as a brake, with slow AIMD on capacity (A):** this host read load 52 with `cpu some` 0.03, so loadavg misleads. Zuul's window is a shipped AIMD precedent. PSI is Linux-only, so keep the loadavg fallback.
3. **Green main first (A):** revert first, auto-bisect after a red full run, no piling on, as Google's TAP does. This is probably the largest gain, but it is unmeasured.
4. **Hub reduction plus a churn-weighted closure ratchet (B):** each avoided hub run saves 20 CPU-hours and needs no dependency. No study measures this directly; the evidence is our log.
5. **Sub-file selection recorded on scheduled full runs, in shadow first (A/B):** file-level selection cannot fix hubs, because every test imports them; Stripe's file-level tracing has the same limit. NameRTS (preprint, Python): 69.9% of test files skipped, safe on 99.6% of commits. Its file-level baseline was safe on only 76.6%, so measure our selector rather than trusting it.
6. **Escape metric and shadow mode (A):** Mozilla, Microsoft and Google all evaluate selection this way. It is cheap, and it makes the other selection changes safe to try.
7. **Full-run cadence budgeted to the host (A):** Meta runs every few hours, Google's Takeout team every 2 h, which cut culprit sets 12x. Here, about 2-3 h or 10 merges; on a laptop, nightly (T).
8. **Measure per-test CPU, then ratchet it (B/T):** 3.9 CPU-s per test is high and I have not profiled why. This may be the biggest linear factor. Add `worksteal` and longest-first ordering.
9. **Size-aware queue with aging and a reservation (A theory):** pure shortest-job-first can starve large runs when sizes vary little, and our jobs can't be preempted.
10. **Passes-only local cache keyed by closure hash (mechanism A, Python C):** I found no measured Python hit rate, and a hermeticity audit is the real cost.

**Recall:** every production system relies on a later full run, not on proving selection safe. Meta misses under 0.1% of faulty changes, and more faults reach its stabilization stage through races than through selection. Elbaum's Google study deferred 20-30% of failures to post-submit. In Shi's study, 38 of 39 missed failures were flaky. Stripe, Mozilla, Microsoft and Launchable publish no escape rates.

**Agents:** I found no study that measures CI load caused by agents. GitHub's 30x capacity target and Stripe's cap of two CI rounds are the best primary evidence.

**Avoid**
- **Raising the constant:** the always-run set already grew from 16 to 23 files.
- **Vegas or Gradient2:** both need dense, uniform samples, and we have about 100 runs a day with 18x cost spread.
- **Loadavg as the only signal.**
- **Trained-model selection:** it needs a labelled history we lack, and hosted forms break local-first.
- **Bazel, Buck2 or Pants as a dependency:** the migration is large; copy the cache-key design instead.
- **A remote cache by default:** it conflicts with r-consent-outward.
- **Depth caps from Google's distance-10 result:** our graph is not comparable.
- **Batching or deep speculation while main is red:** batching reportedly pays only below about 40% build failure (secondary citation), and we are far above that.
- **Auto-disable or retry-until-green:** Slack shows the hidden breakages and the re-enable trap.
- **stet or testmon as hard dependencies:** stet is a research preview, and testmon's per-checkout store does not fit many worktrees.
